src_fact_pattern: Robert and Angela Chen, ages 52 and 48, are a married couple in Portland, Oregon. Robert is a software engineer earning $145,000 annually, and Angela works part-time as a graphic designer earning $38,000. In January 2021, they opened a joint brokerage account with $420,000 — the combined proceeds from an inheritance and the sale of a rental property — with the stated objectives of moderate long-term growth for retirement and their two children's college education. Their advisor, Nathan Bridges, had discretionary authority over the account. Between January 2021 and September 2023, Bridges executed 387 trades in the account, including frequent round-trip transactions in large-cap equities, technology ETFs, and options positions. On 42 separate occasions, a security was purchased and sold within 30 days. On 17 occasions, the same security was sold and then repurchased within two weeks at a similar or higher price. The account's annualized turnover ratio during the 33-month period was approximately 11.2, meaning the entire portfolio was turned over more than 11 times per year. Total commissions and transaction costs generated by the trading activity amounted to $128,600, representing approximately 30.6% of the account's original value. The cost-to-equity ratio — the percentage the account would need to earn annually just to cover the costs of trading — was approximately 34%. Despite this frenzied activity, the account's net value at the end of the period was $291,000, representing a loss of $129,000 (30.7%) of the original investment, while the S&P 500 returned approximately 19% over the same period. Bridges earned $96,400 in personal commissions from the trading. When Robert Chen reviewed his annual statements in October 2023 and questioned the losses, Bridges attributed the decline to 'market volatility' and 'strategic repositioning' and encouraged the Chens to add more capital. The Chens' prior investment experience was limited to employer 401(k) plans invested in target-date funds.
src_red_flag: A discretionary account managed for a moderate-risk couple with long-term goals was subjected to extreme trading frequency generating outsized commissions and severe losses, with the advisor's compensation from commissions vastly exceeding the client's investment returns.

src_regulatory_concern: Excessive trading (churning) violates FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), specifically the quantitative suitability obligation which requires that an advisor with actual or de facto control over an account not engage in trading that is excessive in light of the customer's investment profile. The conduct also violates FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor) as churning is inherently dishonest and constitutes a fraud on the customer. Under SEC Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), the Care Obligation requires that recommendations not place the financial professional's interest ahead of the customer's — generating $96,400 in personal commissions while the account lost $129,000 is a clear violation. The SEC has long held that churning constitutes a violation of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, as it involves a scheme to defraud through excessive trading in an account over which the broker exercises control. The firm's supervision may be deficient under FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision), as automated exception reports should have flagged the turnover ratio and cost-to-equity ratio well before 33 months of trading accumulated. The advisor's misleading explanation attributing the losses to market conditions rather than his own trading activity may constitute additional misrepresentations.
src_recommended_action: The firm's compliance department should immediately revoke Nathan Bridges' discretionary authority over all accounts and place him on heightened supervision pending investigation. An independent trade review should be conducted across all of Bridges' accounts to determine if similar patterns exist with other clients. The firm should calculate disgorgement amounts and proactively offer restitution to the Chens, including the $128,600 in commissions and transaction costs plus the opportunity cost of the foregone market gains. The matter should be reported through the firm's regulatory reporting obligations, including potential filing of a Form U5 amendment if Bridges is terminated. FINRA's automated surveillance systems (such as those monitoring turnover ratios and cost-to-equity ratios) should be supplemented by the firm's own exception reporting thresholds — the firm should review why its internal alerts did not trigger intervention earlier. The Chens should be advised of their right to pursue recovery through FINRA arbitration. The firm should also review its procedures for granting and monitoring discretionary authority, implement hard turnover-ratio alerts that require mandatory supervisory review, and consider restricting commission-based compensation structures for discretionary accounts in favor of fee-based arrangements.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Huang, age 52, is a pediatrician earning $340,000 annually with a net worth of $2.1 million, approximately $900,000 of which is in liquid investment accounts. She has moderate risk tolerance documented on her new account form and a stated investment objective of growth with income. She has 22 years of investing experience, primarily in diversified mutual funds and individual equities. In March 2023, her financial advisor, Derek Paulson at Ridgemont Securities, recommended she invest $135,000 (15% of her liquid portfolio) into a non-traded real estate investment trust focused on medical office buildings and ambulatory surgical centers. Derek conducted substantial due diligence: he reviewed the offering memorandum, analyzed the sponsor's 12-year track record showing consistent 6.8% annual distributions across four prior programs, examined the independent valuation reports, attended the sponsor's due diligence conference, and prepared a written internal memo documenting his analysis. He noted that Margaret's medical background gave her unique insight into the healthcare real estate sector, and that the REIT's projected 6-7% yield complemented her growth-oriented equity holdings by adding income. Margaret's existing portfolio had no alternative investment exposure. The product carried a 7-year expected hold period, early redemption was limited to hardship cases with a 10% penalty in years 1-3, upfront fees totaled 11.5% (including selling commissions and offering costs), and the product was only available to investors meeting accredited investor thresholds. Derek documented the recommendation, provided the prospectus, and Margaret signed all required disclosures including an alternative investment acknowledgment form. Six months later, Margaret needed $200,000 for an unexpected opportunity to buy into a medical practice partnership — a time-sensitive, career-defining opportunity. She discovered she could not access her REIT investment without severe penalties and insufficient liquidity across her remaining portfolio to fund the full amount.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) including all three component obligations: reasonable-basis suitability (Rule 2111.05(a)), customer-specific suitability (Rule 2111.05(b)), and quantitative suitability (Rule 2111.05(c)); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-73 (Non-Traditional Products); FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 (Due Diligence for Non-Traded REITs); Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B) requiring consideration of reasonably available alternatives to the recommendation; FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the extensive due diligence performed. While Derek Paulson satisfied the reasonable-basis suitability obligation under FINRA Rule 2111 (he thoroughly researched the product), and arguably the quantitative suitability component (single concentration at 15%), he failed the customer-specific suitability prong. Under FINRA Rule 2111.05(a), the customer-specific obligation requires the advisor to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is suitable for the particular customer based on that customer's investment profile, including liquidity needs. The critical deficiency is the liquidity analysis. FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-73 and subsequent guidance on alternative investments emphasize that firms must evaluate whether customers can afford to have capital locked up for extended periods. With $900,000 in liquid assets and $135,000 committed to a 7-year illiquid lockup, Margaret retained $765,000 in liquid assets — seemingly adequate. However, the advisor failed to conduct a holistic liquidity needs assessment. As a physician in her early 50s with moderate risk tolerance, Derek should have explored potential near-term capital needs including practice opportunities, which are common career events for physicians. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 specifically addresses due diligence requirements for non-traded REITs, noting that high upfront costs (here 11.5%) create an immediate loss of principal that compounds the illiquidity concern. The combination of the 11.5% front-end load with a 7-year lockup means Margaret's investment would need to earn approximately 1.75% annually just to recover fees before generating any actual return — a fact that tensions against her moderate risk tolerance. The recommendation also potentially runs afoul of Reg BI's Care Obligation under Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B), which requires consideration of reasonably available alternatives. Lower-cost, more liquid REIT alternatives (such as publicly traded healthcare REITs) existed that could have provided similar healthcare real estate exposure with daily liquidity and dramatically lower fees. Derek's memo does not address why the non-traded structure was preferable to these alternatives for this specific client.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because the advisor performed exemplary product-level due diligence — attending conferences, reviewing track records, writing internal memos — which creates a strong surface appearance of compliance. Most general LLMs would focus on the thoroughness of the research and the reasonable concentration level (15%), the client's accredited investor status, her high income, and her medical expertise aligning with the healthcare REIT sector. The trap is that reasonable-basis suitability and customer-specific suitability are distinct obligations, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other. The real violation is subtle: inadequate liquidity needs assessment and failure to consider reasonably available alternatives with better cost/liquidity profiles. The after-the-fact liquidity crisis is a red herring in one sense (you don't judge suitability by hindsight), but it illuminates the pre-existing deficiency in the liquidity analysis that should have been conducted at the time of recommendation.
src_common_wrong_answer: No violation. The advisor conducted thorough due diligence, the client was an accredited investor with high income and significant liquid assets, the 15% allocation was reasonable, the client's medical expertise aligned with the product's sector focus, and the subsequent liquidity need was an unforeseeable event that cannot retroactively make a suitable recommendation unsuitable. All disclosures were provided and signed.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Collins, age 72, is a retired schoolteacher in Tampa, Florida, with a pension of $3,200 per month and total savings of $285,000 in her brokerage account. Her stated risk tolerance is conservative, and her investment objective is capital preservation with modest income generation. Between January 2022 and December 2023, her financial advisor, Derek Paulson, at a mid-sized broker-dealer, executed 14 separate mutual fund switches in Margaret's account. Each switch involved selling one Class A share mutual fund and purchasing another Class A share mutual fund within the same asset category — typically large-cap domestic equity or investment-grade bond funds. Each purchase triggered a new front-end sales load averaging 4.75%, costing Margaret approximately $2,850 per switch. Over the two-year period, Margaret paid roughly $39,900 in front-end loads alone, plus transaction costs. The replacement funds had nearly identical investment objectives, holdings overlap of 70–85%, and comparable expense ratios to the funds that were sold. Performance of the replacement funds was not materially different from the funds sold. Derek earned approximately $19,950 in commissions from the switches. Margaret's account value declined from $285,000 to $238,400 over this period, despite the broad market gaining approximately 12% during the same timeframe. When Margaret questioned the losses at a December 2023 meeting, Derek told her the switches were necessary to 'stay ahead of market shifts' and 'optimize sector allocation.' Margaret had no prior experience with investing beyond her pension and a small savings account.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer:
Yes, Derek Paulson clearly violated applicable standards governing mutual fund switching and churning. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), a broker must have a reasonable basis for believing that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile. Specifically, FINRA Rule 2111 includes quantitative suitability, which requires that a broker who exercises actual or de facto control over a customer account does not engage in excessive trading. Here, 14 switches in 24 months involving funds with 70–85% holdings overlap and identical investment objectives strongly suggests the switches lacked any reasonable basis and were designed to generate commissions rather than benefit the client.

Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), adopted under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, broker-dealers must act in the retail customer's best interest at the time of a recommendation without placing their own financial interest ahead of the customer's. The Care Obligation under Reg BI requires that the broker exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, consider reasonably available alternatives, and ensure costs do not outweigh benefits. Switching between substantially identical mutual funds that triggered $39,900 in redundant front-end loads clearly fails this standard — the costs far exceeded any conceivable benefit.

FINRA has issued extensive guidance on mutual fund switching (e.g., FINRA Regulatory Notices 12-25 and 07-06) warning that switching between funds with similar objectives to generate sales charges is a hallmark violation. The fact that the replacement funds were in the same asset classes, had substantial overlap, and performed comparably to what was sold demonstrates no legitimate investment rationale.

Additionally, FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade) is implicated, as the pattern of self-serving transactions at the expense of a 72-year-old conservative retiree with limited sophistication reflects conduct inconsistent with just and equitable principles of trade.

The likely regulatory outcome would include disgorgement of commissions, restitution to the customer, a fine, and a potential suspension or bar for Derek Paulson. Margaret would also have strong grounds for recovery through FINRA arbitration.

src_fact_pattern: Gloria Tennyson, age 72, is a retired school cafeteria worker living in rural Mississippi. She has a monthly Social Security income of $1,480 and a small pension of $620 per month. In March 2023, she received a $185,000 inheritance from her late sister's estate, which represented the entirety of her liquid savings outside of a $12,000 checking account. Gloria completed only a high school education and had never invested in anything beyond a savings account and a certificate of deposit at her local bank. She described her goals to her advisor, Kevin Draper, as 'keeping the money safe so I can pay for my medications and maybe help my grandkids with college someday.' She told Draper she could not afford to lose any of the inheritance. Draper, a registered representative at a mid-size broker-dealer, recommended that Gloria invest $140,000 into a portfolio of leveraged and inverse exchange-traded products — specifically, $60,000 in a 3x leveraged S&P 500 ETF, $45,000 in a 2x leveraged emerging markets ETF, and $35,000 in an inverse volatility ETN. Draper explained these as 'funds that track the stock market but with extra upside.' He did not explain the daily reset mechanism, compounding decay, or the risk of total principal loss inherent in the inverse volatility product. He also placed $30,000 into a structured note with a 5-year maturity linked to the performance of a basket of biotech stocks, which carried a 2.5% upfront sales commission that was paid to Draper. The remaining $15,000 was placed in a money market fund. Within eight months, the leveraged and inverse positions had lost approximately $67,000 in value due to market volatility and compounding decay. Gloria discovered the losses when she attempted to withdraw funds to pay for a hip replacement surgery.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer: Kevin Draper committed multiple serious violations. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), a broker must have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer based on their investment profile, including age, financial situation, risk tolerance, investment objectives, investment experience, and liquidity needs. Gloria was a 72-year-old unsophisticated retiree with no investment experience, a conservative risk tolerance, stated capital preservation objectives, and limited income. Leveraged and inverse ETFs are complex products that reset daily and are generally considered unsuitable for buy-and-hold investors, particularly elderly investors with no sophistication. FINRA has issued Regulatory Notice 09-31 specifically warning that leveraged and inverse ETFs are typically unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them for longer than one trading session. The inverse volatility ETN carried the risk of near-total loss, which was fundamentally incompatible with Gloria's stated inability to lose her inheritance. Draper also violated the reasonable-basis suitability obligation because he apparently did not understand or chose not to disclose the compounding decay and daily reset mechanics. Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), the Care Obligation requires that a broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, considering the customer's investment profile and the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation. The Disclosure Obligation requires full and fair disclosure of all material facts, including risks. Draper failed both by not explaining the mechanics of these complex products and by characterizing them misleadingly as funds that simply track the market 'with extra upside.' The structured note, with its 5-year lockup, illiquidity, and the 2.5% upfront commission, further raises concerns under Reg BI's Conflict of Interest Obligation, as the commission may have incentivized the recommendation. The concentration of approximately 76% of Gloria's inheritance in high-risk, complex instruments is grossly disproportionate to her profile. A likely regulatory outcome would include disgorgement of commissions, restitution to the customer, a significant fine, and a potential suspension or bar for Draper. The broker-dealer's supervisory obligations under FINRA Rule 3110 may also be implicated if the firm failed to flag these trades for heightened review given the customer's profile.

They listed their risk tolerance as 'moderate to aggressive' and their investment time horizon as 'long-term (10+ years)' on their new account forms. The REIT had a minimum 7-year hold period, no secondary market, and a stated target annual distribution of 6.5%. Priya conducted meaningful due diligence on the REIT: she reviewed the offering memorandum, analyzed the sponsor's 15-year track record (which showed consistent performance across prior vehicles), examined the property portfolio's geographic diversification across 12 states, reviewed third-party appraisals, and confirmed the sponsor had co-invested $50 million of its own capital. Westbrook Wealth Partners' internal policy, documented in its compliance manual, stated that illiquid alternative investments 'should generally not exceed 50% of a client's liquid investable assets, excluding retirement accounts.' The Montoyas' liquid investable assets (taxable account of $420,000 plus cash savings of $250,000) totaled $670,000, making the $200,000 investment approximately 29.9% of liquid investable assets. Priya documented the concentration calculation relative to the firm's policy and noted the investment was within limits. The product paid Priya's firm a 7% upfront commission.

src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — particularly the customer-specific suitability obligation under Rule 2111.04 and .05; Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) Care Obligation if post-June 30, 2020; FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 (guidance on due diligence for non-traded REITs); FINRA Regulatory Notice 15-02 (guidance on alternative investments including illiquidity risks and concentration); applicable state blue sky law concentration limits for non-traded REITs (commonly 10% of net worth excluding primary residence); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor) as it relates to recommending products with outsized commissions when liquid alternatives exist
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the thorough due diligence and compliance with the firm's internal concentration limit. While Priya conducted commendable product-level due diligence (satisfying a 'reasonable basis' suitability analysis under FINRA Rule 2111.04), she failed the 'customer-specific' suitability prong. The Montoyas have college funding needs beginning in 5 years (approximately $125,000-$250,000 per child depending on institution), which creates a material medium-term liquidity need. Locking up $200,000 — nearly half their taxable investment account — in a product with a minimum 7-year hold period directly conflicts with their need to access funds for college in 5 years. Under FINRA Rule 2111's customer-specific obligation, the advisor must consider the customer's 'other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, investment objectives, and any other information the customer may have disclosed.' The time horizon listed as '10+ years' on the new account form pertains to overall retirement planning, but a competent advisor must also consider intermediate financial obligations. Under Regulation BI's Care Obligation (if applicable post-June 30, 2020), the advisor must consider 'reasonably available alternatives' — a traded REIT or other real estate fund with liquidity could have provided similar exposure without the lockup risk. Furthermore, while the investment was within the firm's 50% internal concentration limit for illiquid alternatives, many state securities regulators and product sponsors impose stricter concentration limits — commonly 10% of net worth or liquid net worth — for non-traded REITs specifically. At 9.5% of total net worth, this may technically satisfy some state thresholds, but the more relevant analysis under FINRA guidance (Regulatory Notice 10-22 on non-traded REITs and Regulatory Notice 15-02 on alternative investments) is whether the concentration is suitable given the customer's specific circumstances, not merely whether it clears a numerical threshold. The firm's internal policy using a 50% liquid asset threshold is unusually permissive and does not insulate the advisor from a suitability violation. The 7% upfront commission is also a red flag that should have prompted additional scrutiny of whether this product, versus lower-cost liquid alternatives, was truly in the clients' interest.

A general LLM would likely focus on these factors and conclude no violation occurred. src_fact_pattern: Kevin Ostrowski, age 44, is a software engineer earning $215,000 annually with a net worth of $1.8 million, including $650,000 in a brokerage account. He holds a Series 65 license from a prior stint working at a small advisory firm in 2015-2017, though he is no longer registered and has worked in tech since. Kevin has traded options and futures for personal accounts since 2012, maintaining detailed trading journals and demonstrating consistent understanding of Greeks, volatility surfaces, and portfolio hedging. In January 2024, Kevin contacted his broker, Lisa Fontaine, at a full-service brokerage firm and specifically requested the purchase of $130,000 worth of a 3x leveraged bull semiconductor ETF. He told Lisa he wanted to hold the position for approximately 6 to 8 weeks to capture what he believed would be a short-term rally driven by upcoming earnings season and AI chip demand. He explained that he understood daily rebalancing decay, compounding effects, and volatility drag, and that he was deliberately choosing the leveraged ETF over futures or options because he wanted defined maximum loss (his $130,000 investment) without margin calls. Lisa asked Kevin to confirm his understanding in writing. Kevin sent a detailed email explaining leveraged ETF mechanics, daily reset effects, the impact of volatility on multi-day returns, and his specific thesis with entry/exit criteria. Lisa documented the email, noted Kevin's prior Series 65 licensure, his 12 years of derivatives trading experience, and his $650,000 account size making the $130,000 position a 20% allocation. Lisa also documented that Kevin's stated risk tolerance was aggressive, his investment timeline for this position was 6-8 weeks (not long-term), and his overall portfolio included diversified index funds in retirement accounts totaling $900,000. She executed the trade. Six weeks later, the semiconductor sector experienced a sharp correction and the leveraged ETF lost 58% of its value. Kevin lost approximately $75,400 and filed a complaint alleging Lisa should have refused the trade or steered him toward a non-leveraged semiconductor ETF.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation component; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) as supplementary guidance; FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs, June 2009); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Complex Products and Heightened Suitability Obligations). Note that Notice 09-31 cautions that leveraged ETFs are typically unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them for longer than one trading session, but does not prohibit short-to-intermediate-term tactical use by sophisticated investors who understand the products.
src_correct_answer: No, this is not a violation. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which applies to broker-dealer recommendations after June 30, 2020, Lisa was required to act in Kevin's best interest at the time of the recommendation by satisfying the Care Obligation, Disclosure Obligation, Conflict of Interest Obligation, and Compliance Obligation. Under the Care Obligation, the broker must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the product and have a reasonable basis for believing it is in the customer's best interest based on the customer's investment profile. Here, Lisa met these obligations: (1) Customer-specific suitability/Care Obligation: Kevin is a 44-year-old high-income, high-net-worth investor with aggressive risk tolerance. The $130,000 position represents 20% of his brokerage account and approximately 7.2% of his total net worth—a meaningful but not reckless allocation for an aggressive investor. His remaining portfolio is well-diversified. (2) Reasonable basis: Kevin has 12 years of derivatives trading experience, previously held a Series 65 license, and demonstrated specific, sophisticated understanding of leveraged ETF mechanics including daily rebalancing, volatility drag, and compounding effects—precisely the risks that make leveraged ETFs problematic for unsophisticated investors. His written explanation confirms genuine comprehension, not mere checkbox acknowledgment. (3) Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs), firms and advisors are cautioned that leveraged ETFs are generally unsuitable for long-term buy-and-hold investors because of the compounding effects of daily resets. However, Kevin's stated 6-8 week holding period with defined entry/exit criteria represents exactly the kind of short-to-medium-term tactical use for which these products are designed. He actually held for six weeks, consistent with his stated plan. (4) Lisa's documentation was thorough—she captured the client's written explanation, investment thesis, risk acknowledgment, experience, and time horizon. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation, the advisor is not required to refuse a transaction that is consistent with the customer's stated investment profile and objectives merely because a loss later occurred. The fact that Kevin filed a complaint after losses does not retroactively make the recommendation unsuitable. The client's sophistication, appropriate position sizing, correct holding period, and genuine product understanding all support compliance.
src_why_adversarial: This is a client-direction trap combined with a knowledge trap. General LLMs tend to flag any leveraged ETF recommendation as a violation, particularly after significant losses, because of the well-known general guidance that leveraged ETFs are unsuitable for most retail investors. The trap is that this general guidance from FINRA Notice 09-31 does not create a blanket prohibition—it identifies specific concerns (long-term holding, investor misunderstanding of compounding) that are systematically absent in this fact pattern. An LLM is likely to seize on the 58% loss and the leveraged nature of the product and conclude there was a violation, without recognizing that Kevin's genuine sophistication, appropriate holding period, reasonable position sizing, and aggressive risk tolerance make this a textbook case of appropriate leveraged ETF usage. The prior Series 65 licensure and detailed written explanation are designed to tempt an LLM into dismissing them as insufficient, when they actually constitute strong evidence of genuine customer sophistication.
src_common_wrong_answer: Yes, violation. Leveraged ETFs are inherently unsuitable for retail investors due to daily rebalancing decay and compounding effects. The 58% loss demonstrates the product's extreme risk. Lisa should have recommended a non-leveraged semiconductor ETF or refused the trade. The client's prior Series 65 license from years ago and self-reported experience do not relieve the advisor of her independent obligation to ensure the recommendation is in the client's best interest. A 3x leveraged product with a 20% portfolio allocation is excessive concentration in a speculative instrument.

src_fact_pattern: In March 2023, financial advisor Derek Hollis at Pinnacle Wealth Partners recommended a non-traded real estate investment trust (REIT) to his client, Margaret Yuen, age 71, a retired school principal with a $1.4 million portfolio. Margaret's stated investment objectives were income and preservation of capital. She had a moderate risk tolerance, a 10-year investment horizon, and was drawing $4,200 per month from her portfolio to supplement her pension. Her liquid net worth was $1.4 million, and her annual income from all sources (pension, Social Security) was $62,000. Derek conducted extensive due diligence on the non-traded REIT, named Greystone Healthcare Properties III. He reviewed the prospectus, attended a due diligence seminar hosted by the sponsor, analyzed the underlying healthcare real estate portfolio (which consisted of 14 skilled nursing facilities and 6 medical office buildings), reviewed the sponsor's track record across two prior offerings that had successfully liquidated at gains, and prepared a written memo summarizing his findings. He concluded the product was sound and offered an attractive 6.8% distribution yield. He recommended Margaret invest $280,000 — exactly 20% of her portfolio — into the non-traded REIT. Pinnacle's internal policy permitted alternative investment concentrations up to 25% of liquid net worth for clients with moderate risk tolerance and above. The product had a minimum 5-year hold period with no guaranteed liquidity, and early redemption was limited to 5% of outstanding shares per quarter on a first-come-first-served basis, subject to board discretion. Margaret's remaining portfolio was allocated 45% to investment-grade bonds, 25% to blue-chip dividend stocks, and 10% to a money market fund. Derek documented the recommendation, Margaret signed the alternative investment disclosure form, and the transaction was processed. Six months later, Greystone suspended its share redemption program and cut distributions by 40% due to rising interest rates impacting property valuations.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — specifically 2111.05(a) (reasonable-basis suitability), 2111.05(b) (quantitative suitability), and 2111.05(c) (customer-specific suitability); Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) Care Obligation; FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 (Non-Traded REITs); FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 (Concentration Limits for Illiquid Securities)
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the thorough due diligence. While Derek Hollis satisfied the reasonable-basis suitability obligation (FINRA Rule 2111.05(a)) by conducting genuine product-level due diligence on the non-traded REIT, he failed the customer-specific suitability obligation (FINRA Rule 2111.05(c)). Margaret Yuen is a 71-year-old retiree drawing $4,200/month ($50,400/year) from a $1.4 million portfolio, meaning she depends on portfolio liquidity. Locking up $280,000 (20%) in a non-traded REIT with a 5-year minimum hold, discretionary and capped redemption provisions, and no secondary market creates a significant liquidity mismatch for a client in the distribution phase of retirement. Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 (discussing non-traded REITs) and subsequent guidance in Regulatory Notice 10-22, firms and advisors must pay particular attention to the illiquid nature of these products relative to clients who may need access to funds. Additionally, under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which was fully effective at the time of the March 2023 recommendation, the Care Obligation requires that the advisor exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the risks of the recommendation in light of the customer's specific profile. The fact that Derek did thorough product-level research does not cure the deficiency: the product's illiquidity profile is fundamentally incompatible with Margaret's withdrawal needs. If Margaret needed to access the REIT funds during the suspended redemption period, she would face a severe liquidity crisis, potentially forcing her to liquidate other holdings at inopportune times. The 20% concentration, while within firm policy limits, does not automatically establish suitability — firm thresholds are ceilings, not safe harbors. FINRA has consistently held in enforcement actions that adherence to internal concentration limits does not immunize an advisor from a suitability finding where the customer's individual circumstances warrant a lower concentration.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because the advisor did everything that appears compliant on the surface: extensive product-level due diligence, written documentation, client disclosure signatures, and adherence to the firm's internal concentration policy. A general-purpose LLM is likely to weigh the thorough due diligence heavily and conclude no violation occurred, especially since the 20% allocation was below the firm's 25% cap. The trap is that reasonable-basis suitability and customer-specific suitability are independent obligations — satisfying one does not satisfy the other. The critical deficiency is the liquidity mismatch for a client in active retirement drawdown, which requires specific knowledge of how non-traded REIT suitability analysis works for income-dependent retirees.
src_common_wrong_answer: No violation. The advisor conducted thorough due diligence, the allocation was within the firm's approved concentration limits, the client had moderate risk tolerance and a 10-year horizon, the product offered attractive income consistent with her objectives, and all disclosures were properly executed.

src_fact_pattern: Thomas Keane, age 52, a senior software engineer at Pinnacle Technologies, earned $285,000 annually and had a total liquid net worth of approximately $2.1 million. He held a brokerage account at Clearfield Financial Services and also maintained a separate investment advisory (fee-based) account at the same firm, both managed by advisor Rachel Voss. Thomas's brokerage account was valued at $800,000 and his advisory account at $1.3 million. In January 2023, Thomas emailed Rachel stating he wanted to purchase an additional $650,000 of Pinnacle Technologies stock in his brokerage account using proceeds from selling diversified equity ETFs in that same account. He already held $340,000 of Pinnacle stock in the brokerage account from prior open-market purchases and approximately $900,000 in unvested Pinnacle RSUs and stock options in a separate employer equity plan (not held at Clearfield). If the additional purchase went through, Pinnacle stock would represent approximately $990,000 of his $800,000 brokerage account (he planned to deposit additional cash), roughly 47% of his total liquid net worth — or approximately 63% when including the unvested RSUs/options. Rachel responded by email documenting the concentration risk, noting that a single stock representing over 45% of liquid net worth created significant unsystematic risk, and that if his unvested equity were included, total Pinnacle exposure would approach two-thirds of his wealth. She recommended he limit the additional purchase to $200,000 and instead diversify into a technology sector ETF for the remaining $450,000. Thomas replied firmly: 'I understand the risk. I work at Pinnacle and know this company inside and out. I have high confidence in its growth trajectory. Please proceed with the full $650,000 purchase.' Rachel executed the full purchase, documented Thomas's directive, his rejection of her diversification recommendation, and his stated rationale in her client file. The advisory account remained diversified across multiple asset classes. Six months later, Pinnacle stock dropped 38% following an accounting restatement, and Thomas's position lost approximately $376,000 in value. He filed a complaint alleging overconcentration and failure to protect him from excessive single-stock risk.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: SEC Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1), including the Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), specifically FINRA Rule 2111.03 (exemption for unsolicited customer-directed transactions); SEC Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (IA-5248, June 5, 2019) regarding fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (guidance on customer-directed transactions and documentation requirements)
src_correct_answer: This requires analyzing two separate standards because Thomas held both a brokerage account and an investment advisory account at the same firm. For the BROKERAGE ACCOUNT (where the transaction occurred): Under Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1), which was in effect in January 2023, Rachel had a Care Obligation requiring her to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, and to consider the costs, risks, rewards, and reasonably available alternatives. Critically, under Reg BI, when a customer directs a specific transaction after the broker-dealer has made a different recommendation, the execution of the customer's unsolicited order is generally NOT a 'recommendation' subject to Reg BI. Rachel recommended AGAINST the full purchase and suggested a specific alternative. Thomas rejected the recommendation and directed the trade. Rachel documented the exchange thoroughly. Under FINRA Rule 2111.03, an unsolicited customer-directed transaction is not subject to the suitability requirement. However, there is a nuance: Rachel must not have 'recommended' the purchase. Her emails show she recommended against it. The execution of the client-directed order, with documented rejection of her contrary advice, likely does NOT constitute a violation in the brokerage account context. For the ADVISORY ACCOUNT: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Rachel owes a fiduciary duty to Thomas encompassing a duty of care and duty of loyalty. The fiduciary duty arguably extends to Thomas's overall financial situation, not just the advisory account in isolation. Some interpretive guidance (SEC Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers, June 2019) suggests an advisor must consider the client's complete financial picture. However, the transaction occurred in the brokerage account, and the advisory account remained diversified. The advisor's fiduciary duty in the advisory account does not grant her authority to block a client-directed transaction in a separate brokerage account. Overall: This is likely NOT a violation. Rachel satisfied her obligations by (1) providing a contrary recommendation with specific alternatives, (2) documenting the concentration risk, (3) documenting the client's informed directive, and (4) executing an unsolicited client-directed transaction. The key legal distinction is that client-directed transactions, after proper disclosure and documentation, are not subject to suitability or best interest obligations when the advisor has recommended otherwise.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario creates a powerful trap because the concentration levels (47-63% of liquid net worth in a single stock) are extreme and clearly imprudent from a portfolio theory perspective, which will cause most LLMs to conclude 'violation' based on the outcome and the obvious risk. The multi-party/multi-account structure (brokerage vs. advisory at the same firm) creates confusion about which standard applies and whether fiduciary duty from the advisory account 'bleeds over' to block brokerage transactions. The client-direction trap is the core mechanism: LLMs typically do not distinguish between recommended transactions and unsolicited client-directed transactions, and they often incorrectly state that an advisor 'cannot execute' a trade they believe is unsuitable even when the client directs it after being warned. The advisor's thorough documentation, contrary recommendation, and proposed alternative actually demonstrate exemplary compliance — but the catastrophic loss and extreme concentration make this look like an obvious violation to models that focus on outcomes rather than process.
src_common_wrong_answer: Yes, violation. The advisor should have refused to execute the trade because the resulting concentration of 47-63% in a single stock created excessive unsystematic risk inconsistent with prudent investment management. As a fiduciary (via the advisory relationship) and under best interest obligations (in the brokerage account), the advisor had a duty to protect the client from his own harmful decisions, and merely documenting the risk was insufficient. The advisor should have either refused to execute the trade or escalated to compliance for a block.

src_fact_pattern: Helen Kowalski, age 81, is a widow living in a retirement community in Sarasota, Florida. She has annual income of $36,000 from Social Security and a small annuity, and her total liquid savings are $120,000 in a brokerage account — her only financial cushion beyond her monthly income. Helen's new account form, completed in June 2022, lists her risk tolerance as 'conservative,' her investment objective as 'capital preservation and income,' and her time horizon as 'short-term (1-3 years).' She told her advisor, Marcus Webb, that she needed the money to cover potential assisted living costs if her health declined. In July 2022, Marcus recommended that Helen invest $95,000 — nearly 80% of her liquid assets — into a portfolio of leveraged exchange-traded funds focused on emerging market equities and small-cap biotechnology stocks. These products use 2x and 3x leverage and are designed for short-term tactical trading by sophisticated investors; their prospectuses explicitly state they are not intended to be held for more than one trading day. Marcus told Helen these funds 'had great upside potential' and would 'grow her nest egg quickly.' By December 2022, the portfolio had declined by 41%, losing approximately $38,950. Helen was left with approximately $81,050 in total liquid savings. Marcus earned $2,850 in commissions on the transactions.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer:
Yes, Marcus Webb clearly violated applicable standards. This is a straightforward case of recommending speculative, high-risk products to a conservative, elderly investor.

**Reg BI — Care Obligation:**
Under Regulation Best Interest, Marcus was required to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making his recommendation. An 81-year-old widow with $120,000 in total liquid assets, a conservative risk tolerance, a capital preservation objective, and a need for the funds to cover potential assisted living costs is the prototypical conservative investor. Leveraged ETFs — products explicitly designed for single-day holding periods by sophisticated traders — are categorically inappropriate for this profile. The recommendation fails every element of the customer-specific analysis: it ignores her age, risk tolerance, investment objective, time horizon, liquidity needs, and financial situation.

**FINRA Rule 2111 — Customer-Specific Suitability:**
The customer-specific obligation under Rule 2111 requires that a recommended transaction be suitable for the particular customer based on that customer's investment profile. Helen's profile is entirely inconsistent with leveraged emerging market and biotech ETFs. FINRA has issued specific guidance (Regulatory Notice 09-31 and 09-65) warning that leveraged and inverse ETFs are typically unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them for longer than one trading session, due to the effects of daily rebalancing and volatility decay.

**Reasonable-Basis Suitability:**
Marcus also likely fails reasonable-basis suitability. Any advisor exercising reasonable diligence would understand that 2x and 3x leveraged ETFs carry extreme volatility risk and are unsuitable as core holdings for any investor, let alone a conservative 81-year-old.

**Concentration Risk:**
Placing approximately 80% of Helen's total liquid net worth in speculative leveraged products creates dangerous concentration, leaving her with virtually no diversification or safety net.

**Likely Regulatory Outcome:**
This would be viewed as a clear violation in any enforcement or arbitration proceeding. Marcus would likely face restitution of Helen's losses (approximately $38,950), disgorgement of commissions ($2,850), fines, and a suspension. Given the egregiousness — recommending leveraged ETFs to an 81-year-old conservative investor — a bar from the industry is possible, particularly if this is part of a pattern. Helen would very likely prevail in FINRA arbitration.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Hsu, age 72, retired schoolteacher with $340,000 in savings, walked into a regional broker-dealer office in April 2019 seeking help rolling over her 403(b) into an IRA. She had no investment experience beyond the target-date fund in her 403(b), described her risk tolerance as 'low,' and said she needed the money to supplement her $2,100/month pension. Broker David Cranston recommended she invest $310,000 into a Class A share variable annuity with a 5.75% front-end load ($17,825 in commissions), a 1.35% annual mortality and expense charge, a 0.85% fund management fee, and a 7-year declining surrender charge starting at 7%. Cranston documented that the annuity provided a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit rider (costing an additional 1.10% annually), tax-deferred growth, and downside protection — all of which he noted were suitable for a retiree needing income stability. His firm's product review committee had approved the annuity for retirees in March 2019. The total all-in annual cost was approximately 3.30%. Margaret's 403(b) target-date fund had a total expense ratio of 0.12%. Cranston completed his recommendation and Margaret signed the paperwork on June 14, 2019. The annuity was purchased and funded on June 28, 2019. Margaret filed a complaint in January 2021 alleging excessive fees and an unsuitable recommendation. She noted that she was never told about lower-cost alternatives and that the tax-deferral benefit was meaningless since the IRA was already tax-deferred.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — requiring reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability; FINRA Rule 2330 (Members' Responsibilities Regarding Deferred Variable Annuities) — requiring analysis of whether the customer benefits from tax-deferral features, assessment of total costs, and consideration of the surrender period relative to the customer's liquidity needs. Note: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) does NOT apply because the compliance date was June 30, 2020, and the recommendation occurred in June 2019.
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation, and critically the applicable standard depends on the exact date. Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) became effective on June 30, 2020, but the compliance date was also June 30, 2020, meaning it did not apply to recommendations made before that date. However, the recommendation was made on June 14, 2019, and funded June 28, 2019, so the applicable standard is FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and FINRA Rule 2330 (Variable Annuities). Under FINRA Rule 2330, before recommending the purchase or exchange of a deferred variable annuity, the registered representative must have a reasonable basis to believe the transaction is suitable. Specifically, Rule 2330(b) requires consideration of whether the customer would benefit from the features of a deferred variable annuity (such as tax-deferred growth, annuitization, or a death benefit) in light of the customer's existing tax status. Here, the tax-deferral benefit is redundant because the funds are already in a tax-advantaged IRA — a classic 'tax-deferral stacking' problem that FINRA has repeatedly flagged. The 5.75% front-end load plus 3.30% annual all-in cost on a 72-year-old's retirement savings is excessive when a low-cost target-date fund at 0.12% was available. The 7-year surrender charge effectively locks up the money until Margaret is 79, creating a severe liquidity mismatch with her income needs. While the guaranteed withdrawal rider provides some income certainty, the total cost erodes principal far faster than alternatives. Under FINRA Rule 2111's quantitative suitability component and Rule 2330's specific variable annuity provisions, this recommendation was unsuitable. Even though the firm's product committee approved the annuity, the individual suitability determination for this specific customer was deficient. The advisor also arguably violated the customer-specific obligation under Rule 2111(a) by failing to consider reasonably available lower-cost alternatives that achieved the same goals.
src_why_adversarial: A general LLM is likely to apply Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) to this fact pattern because the complaint was filed in January 2021, well after Reg BI's June 30, 2020 compliance date. However, the recommendation and transaction occurred in June 2019, before Reg BI applied. The correct standard is FINRA's suitability rule and variable annuity rule. Additionally, the firm's product committee approval and the advisor's documented rationale (guaranteed income, downside protection) create a veneer of compliance that could fool a model. The subtlety is that tax-deferral stacking inside an IRA is a well-known red flag under FINRA Rule 2330 that general LLMs often miss, and the temporal question of which standard applies is a common trap.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely analyze this under Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation and Cost component, concluding it is a violation under Reg BI because the advisor failed to consider lower-cost alternatives. While the conclusion (violation) is correct, the legal basis would be wrong — Reg BI did not apply to transactions completed in June 2019. Some models might also find no violation, reasoning that the advisor documented the benefits of the guaranteed income rider and the firm approved the product, overlooking the specific variable annuity suitability requirements and the tax-deferral stacking issue.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Ellison, age 62, is a recently retired school principal with a $1.2 million portfolio consisting primarily of municipal bonds and blue-chip dividend stocks. Her account documents indicate a moderate risk tolerance, a primary goal of income generation in retirement, and a secondary goal of capital preservation. She has a pension covering roughly 60% of her living expenses, and her investment portfolio is expected to cover the remaining 40%. Her annual income need from the portfolio is approximately $48,000. In March 2023, her financial advisor, Derek Huang, recommended she invest $180,000 — approximately 15% of her portfolio — into a market-linked structured note tied to the S&P 500 with a 6-year maturity. The note offered a 9.2% annual coupon contingent on the S&P 500 not declining more than 30% from its initial level on any quarterly observation date. If the index breached that 30% barrier at any point, the coupon for that quarter would not be paid and, at maturity, the investor's principal could be reduced by the full percentage decline of the index. The note was issued by a large, investment-grade bank with a credit rating of A-. Derek explained the barrier feature and the conditional coupon structure to Margaret during two separate meetings, and she signed a product-specific disclosure acknowledging the risks, including the possibility of losing a substantial portion of principal. Margaret's account records show she had previously held a small allocation (about 4%) in a callable corporate bond with a BBB+ rating, and she had once invested $30,000 in a real estate investment trust with a 7-year lock-up period. Derek's internal notes state that Margaret expressed frustration with the low yields on her municipal bonds (averaging 3.1%) and specifically asked about ways to boost her income without taking on 'too much stock market risk.' The structured note's conditional coupon of 9.2% would generate approximately $16,560 annually if all coupons were paid, meaningfully supplementing her income. Derek did not present alternative options such as higher-yielding corporate bond funds, preferred stock ETFs, or dividend growth strategies during the documented meetings, though he later stated in a supervisory review that he had verbally discussed alternatives. Margaret's remaining portfolio of approximately $1.02 million continued to generate roughly $35,000 in annual income from dividends and bond interest.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_analysis: Arguments that Derek violated suitability or best interest standards: The structured note's 6-year maturity and contingent coupon structure introduce significant complexity and downside risk for a 62-year-old retiree whose primary goal is income generation and capital preservation. A 30% barrier, while seemingly distant, was tested during market downturns in recent years, and if breached, Margaret could lose both her coupon income and a substantial portion of her $180,000 principal — a meaningful blow to a retiree relying on her portfolio for living expenses. The 15% concentration in a single structured product tied to one index and one issuer's credit introduces both market risk and credit risk that may be disproportionate for her profile. The lack of documented alternatives is concerning; under heightened standards applicable to complex products, advisors are generally expected to demonstrate they considered reasonably available alternatives. Margaret's stated desire to avoid 'too much stock market risk' arguably conflicts with a product whose principal is fully exposed to equity market declines beyond the barrier. Arguments that Derek acted appropriately: Margaret's risk tolerance was listed as moderate, not conservative, and she had prior experience with illiquid and slightly below-investment-grade products, suggesting she was not a purely conservative investor unfamiliar with complexity. The 9.2% conditional coupon directly addressed her stated need for higher income, and the 30% barrier provided a meaningful cushion before principal was at risk. The remaining 85% of her portfolio remained in conservative holdings, and even without the structured note's income, she could cover approximately 89% of her total living expenses through her pension and portfolio income. The issuing bank's A- credit rating was strong, mitigating credit risk. Derek held two meetings to explain the product and obtained signed disclosures, suggesting meaningful informed consent. Margaret's own frustration with low yields and her request for enhanced income arguably invited a recommendation of this nature. The 15% allocation, while notable, is not extreme concentration for a single investment type.
src_why_borderline: This scenario is genuinely ambiguous because the structured note's risk-return profile partially aligns with Margaret's stated income goals and moderate risk tolerance, and the barrier provides downside protection up to a point. However, the product's complexity, the 6-year illiquidity, the contingent nature of the income stream, and the potential for significant principal loss all create tension with her retirement income needs and capital preservation goals. The lack of documented alternatives is a procedural deficiency that could be dispositive in some regulatory frameworks but not others. Reasonable practitioners could disagree about whether 15% in a single structured note crosses the line for a moderate-risk retiree with a pension backstop.
src_borderline_factors: ["Client's moderate (not conservative) risk tolerance and prior experience with mildly complex/illiquid products", "15% allocation is meaningful but not extreme concentration", "Conditional coupon directly addresses client's stated income frustration and need", "30% barrier provides cushion but does not eliminate significant principal risk", "6-year maturity creates illiquidity for a 62-year-old with ongoing income needs", "Pension covers 60% of expenses, reducing but not eliminating dependence on portfolio income", "Lack of documented alternative product analysis despite verbal claims", "Client affirmatively requested higher-income options, arguably providing informed direction", "Signed product-specific risk disclosure obtained after two explanatory meetings"]
src_likely_outcome: A regulator would likely issue a cautionary finding or a modest sanction rather than a severe enforcement action. The core recommendation is defensible given the client's moderate risk tolerance, pension backstop, income needs, and the product's barrier cushion. However, the failure to document consideration of less complex alternatives — particularly under frameworks that require comparative analysis for complex products — would draw scrutiny. The most likely outcome is a finding of a procedural deficiency in the recommendation process, potentially resulting in enhanced supervision requirements or a small fine, rather than a finding that the recommendation itself was fundamentally unsuitable. If the market performed poorly and Margaret actually suffered losses, regulators would be more inclined to find a violation retroactively, illustrating outcome bias in enforcement.
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) requires that a recommended transaction be suitable based on the customer's investment profile, including risk tolerance, financial situation, needs, and other factors. For broker-dealers, Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 Section 15(l) imposes a best interest standard with a Care Obligation requiring the advisor to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, including consideration of reasonably available alternatives. FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 provides specific guidance on heightened suitability obligations for complex products like structured notes, emphasizing that firms must perform reasonable due diligence to understand the product's risks and ensure there is a reasonable basis for the recommendation. The SEC has also issued investor bulletins warning about the risks of structured notes, including credit risk, market risk, and liquidity risk, which factor into the reasonableness analysis.

src_fact_pattern: Dorothy Kessler, age 72, retired schoolteacher, visited Harborview Financial Services in January 2024 seeking help with her $680,000 retirement portfolio, which consisted entirely of bank CDs earning 4.8% APY. Dorothy's sole income was Social Security of $2,400/month and her CD interest, which together covered her $4,100/month living expenses. She told her advisor, Natalie Chen, that she was 'very conservative,' that she 'could not afford to lose principal,' and that she needed 'reliable monthly income to pay bills.' Her account documents listed her investment objective as 'income,' risk tolerance as 'conservative,' time horizon as '10+ years' (life expectancy), and annual income need from the portfolio of approximately $22,000. Natalie, who had 12 years of experience and held the Certified Financial Planner designation, conducted a thorough analysis. She noted that CD rates had peaked and the Federal Reserve was widely expected to begin cutting rates in 2024, which would reduce Dorothy's CD income upon maturity. Natalie prepared a written proposal recommending Dorothy move $510,000 (75% of the portfolio) into a diversified portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds and U.S. Treasury bonds with laddered maturities from 2 to 10 years, yielding a weighted average of 5.1%. The remaining $170,000 would stay in a high-yield savings account as a liquidity reserve. Natalie's analysis showed the bond ladder would generate approximately $26,000 in annual interest income — exceeding Dorothy's $22,000 need — and that all bonds were rated A or higher. Natalie documented her reasoning in a detailed written memorandum, including the rate-cut risk to CDs, the credit quality of each bond, the laddered structure to manage reinvestment risk, and the liquidity reserve. The bonds were purchased at par or slight premiums. Natalie charged a one-time commission of 1.2% on the bond purchases ($6,120 total) with no ongoing advisory fee. Dorothy signed all disclosures and agreed to the plan. Over the next 10 months, interest rates declined by 75 basis points, and Dorothy's bond portfolio continued paying the locked-in coupons. However, Dorothy filed a complaint alleging that Natalie should not have moved her out of FDIC-insured CDs, that she was exposed to credit risk she didn't want, and that the $6,120 commission was excessive.

src_correct_answer: No, this is likely not a violation. Natalie's recommendation was both suitable and consistent with the customer's best interest. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the recommendation must have a reasonable basis, must be suitable for the specific customer, and must not involve excessive activity. Natalie satisfied reasonable-basis suitability by conducting a thorough analysis of rate-cut risk to Dorothy's existing CD income, selecting investment-grade (A-rated or higher) bonds to minimize credit risk, laddering maturities to manage reinvestment risk, and maintaining a substantial liquidity reserve. Customer-specific suitability was met because the bond ladder actually increased Dorothy's income from roughly $22,000 to $26,000 while preserving conservative positioning: investment-grade bonds with laddered maturities are a classic conservative income strategy. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1), the Care Obligation requires the advisor to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, consider reasonably available alternatives, and ensure the recommendation is in the customer's best interest without placing the advisor's interest ahead of the customer's. Natalie documented her analysis, considered the alternative of staying in CDs (which carried reinvestment risk given the rate environment), and chose a well-matched conservative strategy. The 1.2% one-time commission on bond purchases is within industry norms and is not excessive under FINRA markup/markdown guidance (FINRA Rule 2121), which generally considers 5% as a benchmark for equity transactions and recognizes that bond commissions vary but 1-2% is standard for individual bond purchases. The Disclosure Obligation under Reg BI was met through Dorothy's signed disclosures. While Dorothy lost FDIC insurance, moving from CDs to A-rated bonds is a modest and well-documented step that addresses a real risk (rate cuts reducing future CD income) and is consistent with a conservative income objective. Dorothy's post-hoc complaint reflects an outcome-based grievance rather than a process-based deficiency.
src_why_adversarial: A general LLM is likely to side with the elderly, conservative customer and find a violation because: (1) the advisor moved a 72-year-old retiree out of FDIC-insured instruments, which sounds aggressive; (2) there is an emotional bias toward protecting elderly investors; (3) the client explicitly said she 'could not afford to lose principal' and bonds do carry credit and market risk. However, the recommendation was actually textbook-appropriate — investment-grade bond ladders are among the most common and conservative strategies for income-seeking retirees, the advisor's documentation was thorough, and the rate environment justified the move. The trap is that the advisor did extensive research and reached the RIGHT conclusion for this client, but a surface-level analysis focused on the loss of FDIC insurance and the client's stated conservatism would incorrectly flag this as unsuitable.
src_common_wrong_answer: Yes, violation. Dorothy explicitly stated she could not afford to lose principal and was very conservative. Moving 75% of a 72-year-old retiree's portfolio out of FDIC-insured CDs into bonds that carry credit risk and interest rate risk was inconsistent with her stated objectives. The advisor prioritized generating a commission over the client's clearly expressed preference for safety.

src_fact_pattern: Marcus Webb, a registered representative at a small introducing broker-dealer, had a long-standing client named Raymond Cho, a 44-year-old software engineer earning $195,000 per year with a net worth of approximately $1.2 million, excluding his primary residence. Raymond maintained two accounts with Marcus: a diversified brokerage account worth $680,000 containing index funds and blue-chip equities, and a separate speculative account funded with $45,000 that Raymond described as 'play money I can afford to lose entirely.' In October 2023, Raymond emailed Marcus asking him to purchase 500,000 shares of GreenVolt Micro Corp (ticker: GVMC), a company trading at $0.0038 per share on the OTC Pink Sheets with a market capitalization of approximately $1.9 million. Raymond explained he had been following the company on social media investor forums and believed its experimental solid-state battery technology would be acquired by a major automaker. Marcus pulled up the company's filings and found that GreenVolt had no revenue for the past three fiscal years, had $12,000 in total assets, had received a going concern opinion from its auditor, and that the CEO had a prior bankruptcy. Marcus called Raymond, disclosed all of these findings verbally, and explained that the stock was highly speculative and could go to zero. Raymond responded, 'I understand all of that. This is exactly what the speculative account is for. I've done my own research and I want to buy it. Please execute the trade.' Marcus then sent Raymond the firm's penny stock risk disclosure document, which Raymond signed and returned electronically the same day. Marcus executed the purchase for $1,900 plus a $75 commission. Three months later, GVMC was halted by regulators for suspected market manipulation by company insiders. The stock became worthless. Raymond did not file a complaint, but the firm's compliance department flagged the trade during a routine review and questioned whether Marcus should have refused to execute it.

src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including Supplementary Material .03 (recommended vs. unsolicited transactions); SEC Penny Stock Rules: Exchange Act Rules 15g-1 through 15g-9 (17 CFR §§ 240.15g-1 to 240.15g-9), particularly Rule 15g-2 (risk disclosure), Rule 15g-9 (suitability determination for penny stocks), and Rule 15g-1(e) (established customer exemption); SEC Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1, Care Obligation; FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade).
src_correct_answer: No, Marcus likely did not violate applicable suitability or best interest requirements, though the analysis requires careful attention to penny stock-specific obligations. Under FINRA Rule 2111, a recommendation must be suitable, but when a customer directs a specific unsolicited transaction, the suitability rule generally does not apply to the same degree — FINRA Rule 2111.03 provides that the suitability obligation applies to recommended transactions and strategies. If Raymond independently identified and requested the specific penny stock purchase without Marcus's recommendation, it would be classified as an unsolicited trade, and the standard suitability analysis would not apply. However, penny stocks trigger additional requirements under the SEC's penny stock rules (Exchange Act Rules 15g-1 through 15g-9, codified at 17 CFR §§ 240.15g-1 to 240.15g-9). These rules require broker-dealers to: (1) approve the customer's account for penny stock transactions by obtaining information about the customer's financial situation, investment experience, and objectives (Rule 15g-9(b)); (2) provide a standardized risk disclosure document (Rule 15g-2); (3) provide a disclosure of current quotation and compensation information (Rules 15g-3 and 15g-4); and (4) provide monthly account statements (Rule 15g-6). Critically, Rule 15g-9(c) also requires the broker to make an individualized written determination that the penny stock transaction is suitable for the customer based on the information obtained. However, Rule 15g-1 provides exemptions from these requirements, and Rule 15g-1(e) exempts transactions where the customer is an 'established customer' — defined as someone who has had an account with the broker for at least one year or has made three prior penny stock purchases. If Raymond qualifies as an established customer, the suitability determination under Rule 15g-9 would not be required. If Raymond is NOT an established customer for penny stock purposes, Marcus would need to have made and documented the written suitability determination under Rule 15g-9. On the facts, Marcus appears to have complied: he researched the company, disclosed the risks, provided the penny stock risk disclosure document, and the customer's financial profile (speculative account representing less than 4% of liquid net worth, customer acknowledged risk of total loss, high income earner) supports a finding that the penny stock purchase was suitable for the speculative portion of Raymond's portfolio. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), if this were considered a recommendation, the Care Obligation would require consideration of costs, risks, and the customer's investment profile — but again, the $1,900 position in a designated speculative account for a client with $1.2M net worth and explicit risk acknowledgment appears to satisfy this standard. The trade was appropriate for the customer's stated speculative objective and represented de minimis portfolio risk.
src_why_adversarial: This is a client direction trap combined with a knowledge trap. Most LLMs would either (1) say it's a clear violation because penny stocks are inherently unsuitable for any customer and the advisor should have refused, not knowing that the suitability analysis accounts for designated speculative accounts and proportional risk, or (2) would simply say 'unsolicited trades don't require suitability analysis' without knowing about the special penny stock suitability determination required under Rule 15g-9, which applies even to unsolicited trades unless an exemption applies. The correct answer requires knowledge of the penny stock rules as a separate overlay on top of standard suitability, the established customer exemption, and the nuance that a small speculative allocation for a high-net-worth client can be suitable even for extremely risky securities.
src_common_wrong_answer: Most LLMs would say this is a violation, reasoning that penny stocks with no revenue, minimal assets, and a going concern opinion are per se unsuitable, and that the advisor had a duty to refuse the trade regardless of the client's direction. They would cite the red flags (no revenue, prior CEO bankruptcy, social media sourcing) as evidence the advisor should have overridden the client's wishes, not recognizing that proper disclosure, the unsolicited nature, the proportional allocation, and the client's financial profile collectively support compliance.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Olsen, age 74, is a retired elementary school teacher living in Boise, Idaho. She has a fixed monthly income of $2,800 from her pension and $1,450 from Social Security. Her total liquid savings amount to $185,000, held primarily in a money market account and a certificate of deposit ladder. She has no other sources of income and relies on her savings to cover medical expenses and supplement her monthly living costs. On her new account form, she indicated a 'conservative' risk tolerance, 'preservation of capital' as her primary investment objective, and a time horizon of 3-5 years. She told her advisor, Craig Donnelly, that she could not afford to lose any significant portion of her savings. In March 2024, Donnelly recommended that Margaret move $110,000 — roughly 59% of her liquid savings — into a portfolio consisting of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and two smaller-cap altcoins (Solana and Avalanche). Donnelly told her that 'crypto is the future of money' and that she could expect annual returns of 40% or more. He did not discuss the extreme price volatility of digital assets, the lack of insurance protections on the crypto exchange he recommended, or the possibility that she could lose a substantial portion of her investment. He also did not discuss any alternative investments that might align with her stated objectives. Within four months, the portfolio had declined by approximately $46,000, a 42% loss. Margaret was forced to liquidate at a loss to pay for an emergency surgery, receiving back only $64,000 of her original $110,000 investment.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer: Yes, Craig Donnelly clearly violated applicable suitability and best interest standards. Under FINRA Rule 2111, a broker must have a reasonable basis for believing that a recommendation is suitable for a particular customer based on the customer's investment profile, including age, financial situation, risk tolerance, investment objectives, time horizon, and liquidity needs. Margaret's profile — a 74-year-old retiree with limited fixed income, conservative risk tolerance, capital preservation objectives, and a short time horizon — is fundamentally incompatible with a concentrated allocation to highly volatile cryptocurrency assets. The recommendation to place 59% of her liquid savings into crypto violated the customer-specific suitability obligation (Rule 2111.05(c)) because the investment bore no reasonable relationship to her stated needs. Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), the Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) requires that a broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making a recommendation, including understanding the risks and rewards of the recommended security and having a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest at the time it is made. Donnelly failed on all counts: he did not consider less risky alternatives, he made exaggerated performance projections (40% annual returns), he failed to disclose material risks including volatility and lack of exchange insurance, and he concentrated an elderly client's savings in one of the most speculative asset classes available. Additionally, under FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), projecting 40% annual returns without adequate basis could constitute misleading communications. The quantitative concentration — 59% in a single speculative asset class — also raises concerns under the concentration suitability component. A FINRA arbitration panel or regulatory enforcement action would very likely find multiple violations. Probable outcomes include disgorgement of commissions, compensatory damages to the customer for the $46,000 loss plus opportunity costs, potential punitive sanctions, a fine, and a suspension or bar for the advisor depending on his disciplinary history.
