src_fact_pattern: Robert and Linda Chen, ages 68 and 65 respectively, retired from their careers in January 2023 and met with their financial advisor, Jason Whitfield, at a regional broker-dealer in Charlotte, North Carolina, to restructure their $2.8 million in combined retirement savings. The Chens explained that they needed to begin drawing $9,500 per month from their portfolio starting in July 2023 — just six months away — to cover their mortgage, health insurance premiums, and daily living expenses. They told Whitfield they had no pension, that their combined Social Security income of $4,200 per month would not cover their expenses, and that they could not afford to see significant fluctuations in the value of the money they would need over the next one to five years. They explicitly asked Whitfield to keep the portfolio 'safe and accessible.' Between February and April 2023, Whitfield invested approximately $2.3 million — 82% of the Chens' total portfolio — into long-duration fixed income instruments, including $900,000 in 30-year zero-coupon Treasury STRIPS, $750,000 in a leveraged closed-end fund holding 25-year mortgage-backed securities, and $650,000 in long-dated investment-grade corporate bonds with maturities ranging from 2045 to 2053. The remaining $500,000 was placed in a high-yield bond fund with an average duration of 9.2 years. Whitfield told the Chens that because these were 'all bonds,' the portfolio was conservative. He did not explain duration risk, the inverse relationship between interest rates and bond prices, or the fact that the Federal Reserve had been raising rates aggressively throughout 2022 and into 2023. By October 2023, rising interest rates had caused the portfolio to decline by approximately $520,000, a loss of 18.6%. The 30-year zero-coupon STRIPS alone lost roughly 28% of their value. When the Chens attempted to begin their $9,500 monthly withdrawals, they were forced to sell holdings at substantial losses. The leveraged closed-end fund was trading at a 14% discount to its net asset value, compounding the liquidation losses. Over the next eight months, the Chens withdrew approximately $76,000 while realizing losses of over $190,000 on the sold positions. By mid-2024, their remaining portfolio had fallen to approximately $2.05 million, and they were considering selling their home to meet ongoing expenses. The Chens retained an attorney after learning from an independent advisor that their portfolio's effective duration of approximately 18 years was wildly inconsistent with their six-month-to-five-year income needs.
src_red_flag: Massive mismatch between the clients' near-term income needs beginning in six months and a portfolio constructed almost entirely of long-duration and leveraged fixed income instruments with extreme sensitivity to rising interest rates.
src_red_flag_indicators: ["82% of portfolio invested in bonds with maturities of 25 to 30 years despite income needs beginning within six months", "Portfolio effective duration of approximately 18 years for clients requiring liquidity within 1 to 5 years", "Inclusion of 30-year zero-coupon STRIPS, the most duration-sensitive Treasury instrument available, for clients needing near-term cash flow", "Use of a leveraged closed-end fund holding long-dated mortgage-backed securities, amplifying both interest rate risk and liquidity risk", "No allocation to short-duration instruments, money market funds, or a cash ladder to meet the stated $9,500 monthly withdrawal requirement", "Advisor described the portfolio as 'conservative' based solely on the bond label without explaining duration, interest rate sensitivity, or leverage risk", "Investments made during a well-publicized aggressive rate-hiking cycle, increasing the probability of near-term principal losses on long-duration holdings", "Clients were forced to liquidate positions at losses to fund basic living expenses, including selling a leveraged fund at a 14% discount to NAV"]
src_regulatory_concern: This conduct raises significant concerns under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), particularly the customer-specific and reasonable-basis suitability components: the advisor failed to match the investment time horizon and liquidity profile to the customers' clearly articulated needs. Regulation Best Interest under Section 15(l) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 imposes a Care Obligation requiring the advisor to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in understanding the investment risks and ensuring the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest — constructing a long-duration portfolio for clients with imminent income needs plainly fails this standard. The Disclosure Obligation under Reg BI was also likely violated, as the advisor did not explain duration risk, leverage risk, or the impact of the rising rate environment. FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor) is implicated by the misleading characterization of the portfolio as 'conservative.' FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 specifically addresses duration risk in fixed income recommendations and the obligation to consider interest rate sensitivity in the context of the customer's investment horizon. The firm may have violated FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) if its surveillance systems failed to flag the extreme duration mismatch between the clients' documented short-term liquidity needs and the portfolio's construction.
src_recommended_action: The firm should immediately assign a senior compliance officer to review all documentation related to the Chens' account, including the new account form, investment objectives, risk tolerance disclosures, and any notes from meetings with Whitfield. The firm should conduct a broader review of all of Whitfield's client accounts for similar duration mismatches, particularly among retired or near-retirement clients with documented short-term income needs. src_fact_pattern: Margaret Helms, age 58, a retired schoolteacher with $410,000 in a brokerage account, had been invested in the Vanguard Growth Index Fund (Class A shares) since 2014. Her stated objectives were long-term growth and capital preservation, with a moderate risk tolerance. In March 2019, her longtime advisor, Paul Denton, recommended she switch from the Vanguard Growth Index Fund into the Fidelity Contrafund (Class A shares), citing Fidelity's stronger 3-year performance numbers. Margaret paid a 5.25% front-end load on the new purchase totaling $21,525. The Fidelity fund had a similar expense ratio (0.86% vs. 0.80%) and overlapping top-10 holdings with her existing fund. Six months later, in September 2019, Paul recommended another switch from the Fidelity Contrafund into the T. Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth Fund (Class A shares), again citing recent outperformance. Margaret paid another front-end load of 5.75%, totaling $22,713.75 on the $395,000 balance. Paul documented in his notes each time that the new fund had superior trailing returns and that Margaret verbally agreed to the switches. Paul's firm changed its supervisory framework and compliance obligations effective June 30, 2020, but the transactions all occurred before that date. Paul received the standard dealer concession on each transaction. Margaret's account value at the end of 2019 was $388,200, representing a net loss of $21,800 from her starting balance, while a hypothetical buy-and-hold in the original Vanguard fund would have yielded approximately $445,000 over the same period. Margaret filed a complaint in January 2021, alleging the switches were unnecessary and costly.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), FINRA Rule 2111.05(a) (Quantitative Suitability), FINRA Rule 2111.05(b) (Customer-Specific Suitability), NASD IM-2310-2 (Fair Dealing with Customers — Switching), FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (Suitability and Mutual Fund Transactions), FINRA Regulatory Notice 07-06 (Mutual Fund Switching). Note: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) is NOT applicable because its effective date of June 30, 2020, postdates the transactions.
src_correct_answer: Yes, Paul Denton violated the applicable suitability standard. Because both switches occurred before June 30, 2020 — the effective date of Regulation Best Interest — the transactions are governed by FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and specifically FINRA Rule 2111.05(a), which addresses quantitative suitability, and NASD IM-2310-2 (now incorporated into FINRA guidance), which specifically addresses mutual fund switching. Under the FINRA switching standard, a representative recommending a switch from one mutual fund to another must have a reasonable basis to believe the switch is suitable after considering: (1) the expense differential, including surrender charges and new sales loads; (2) whether the customer has a short-term or long-term investment horizon; (3) the similarity of the existing and recommended funds; and (4) any tax implications. Here, the two switches generated over $44,000 in front-end loads on substantially similar large-cap growth funds with nearly identical expense ratios and overlapping holdings. Paul's sole documented justification — slightly superior trailing returns — is insufficient because past performance does not constitute a reasonable basis for incurring duplicative sales charges, particularly when the funds are functionally interchangeable. The quantitative cost of the switches ($44,238.75 in loads alone) against a $410,000 account represents roughly 10.8% of account value consumed by transaction costs in six months, which is facially unreasonable. Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25, the switch analysis must examine whether the customer would recoup the new sales charges within a reasonable time frame, which was not demonstrated. Even though Reg BI (effective June 30, 2020) would apply a heightened standard, it is not the governing standard here — FINRA Rule 2111 alone is sufficient to find a violation. Paul's receipt of dealer concessions also creates an undisclosed conflict under FINRA Rule 2111.05(b) (customer-specific suitability) since the recommendations served his financial interest at the customer's expense.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is a temporal trap because general LLMs are likely to analyze the complaint (filed January 2021) under Regulation Best Interest, which became effective June 30, 2020. However, the relevant transactions occurred in March 2019 and September 2019 — both before Reg BI's effective date. The correct governing standard is FINRA Rule 2111 and associated switching guidance, not Reg BI. Additionally, LLMs may be tempted to find the switches acceptable because the advisor documented his rationale and obtained client consent, but documented trailing performance alone is legally insufficient to justify switches between substantially similar funds with duplicative loads.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely analyze this under Regulation Best Interest (since the complaint was filed in 2021) and either apply the wrong standard or conclude the advisor met his obligations because he documented performance comparisons and obtained verbal consent for each transaction. Some models might also incorrectly focus on whether the individual funds were 'suitable' in isolation rather than analyzing the switch itself and its associated costs.

src_fact_pattern: Thomas Brennan, age 58, is a senior project manager at an engineering firm in Charlotte, North Carolina, earning $145,000 annually. He has $620,000 in a brokerage account, $380,000 in his employer's 401(k), and $85,000 in savings. His home has a remaining mortgage balance of $110,000. Thomas told his financial advisor, Sarah Liu, that he plans to retire at 65 and wants a balanced approach — he is comfortable with moderate risk and wants both growth and income from his portfolio. He described himself as an experienced investor who has managed his own accounts in the past and understands that higher yields come with higher risk. He specifically asked Sarah about high-yield corporate bonds to boost the income component of his portfolio. After conducting a thorough review of Thomas's financial situation, Sarah recommended allocating 12% of his $620,000 brokerage account ($74,400) to a diversified high-yield corporate bond mutual fund with an average credit rating of BB, an expense ratio of 0.55%, and a yield of approximately 6.8%. The remaining portfolio was allocated as follows: 40% in a diversified U.S. equity index fund, 15% in an international developed markets equity fund, 25% in an investment-grade intermediate-term bond fund, and 8% in a short-term Treasury fund for liquidity. Sarah provided Thomas with the fund's prospectus, discussed the credit risk and potential for default within high-yield bond portfolios, explained that high-yield bonds tend to be more correlated with equities during market stress, and documented the conversation and Thomas's acknowledgment of these risks in her client file. Over the following 12 months, the high-yield bond fund returned 7.2%, and the overall portfolio gained approximately 9.4%.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer:
No, Sarah Liu acted in compliance with applicable standards and made a suitable, well-reasoned recommendation. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the recommendation satisfies all three components. Reasonable-basis suitability is met because Sarah demonstrated an understanding of the product — a diversified high-yield bond mutual fund with an average BB credit rating and a reasonable 0.55% expense ratio — and its risks, including credit risk, default risk, and equity correlation during downturns. Customer-specific suitability is met because Thomas's profile supports this allocation: he is 58 years old with 7 years to retirement, earns a strong income, has over $1 million in total assets across accounts, carries only modest debt, has moderate risk tolerance, seeks both growth and income, is an experienced investor, and specifically requested exposure to high-yield bonds. A 12% allocation to high-yield bonds within a well-diversified portfolio is a proportionate and reasonable position for this investor profile. Quantitative suitability is not at issue as there is no excessive trading.

Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), the Care Obligation is satisfied because Sarah exercised diligence in understanding Thomas's profile, considered the allocation in the context of his overall portfolio, chose a diversified fund rather than individual junk bonds (reducing issuer-specific risk), and ensured the cost (0.55% expense ratio) was reasonable relative to alternatives. The Disclosure Obligation is satisfied because Sarah provided the prospectus, explained credit risk, default potential, and the correlation behavior of high-yield bonds during market stress, and documented these disclosures. The Conflict of Interest Obligation would be satisfied assuming the firm's conflict mitigation policies were followed and no undisclosed compensation incentives favored this particular fund.

If Sarah acted in an investment advisory capacity, her fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 would also be satisfied, as the recommendation was in the client's best interest, appropriately sized, well-disclosed, and aligned with the client's stated objectives and risk tolerance.

The thorough documentation of the risk discussion and the client's informed consent further supports compliance. No regulatory action would be expected.

src_fact_pattern: In September 2022, married couple James and Patricia Donovan, both age 58, had a combined liquid net worth of $1.8 million, annual household income of $245,000, and planned to retire in 7 years. They worked with two different financial professionals at two different firms. Patricia's advisor, Karen Webb at Firm A (a registered investment adviser), managed Patricia's $900,000 IRA and recommended she invest $135,000 (15% of her portfolio) into a non-traded REIT focused on commercial office properties. The REIT had a minimum 5-year hold period, no secondary market, estimated annual distributions of 6.5%, and a 12% upfront load (split between selling commissions, dealer manager fees, and offering costs). Webb documented that Patricia's long time horizon (7+ years), moderate risk tolerance, and desire for income diversification supported the allocation. Separately, James's advisor, Tom Alvarez at Firm B (a broker-dealer), managed James's $900,000 brokerage account. Alvarez, unaware of Webb's recommendation, also recommended a $135,000 investment in a different non-traded REIT — this one focused on industrial warehouses — with similar terms: 6-year hold, no liquidity, 5.8% projected distributions, and an 11% upfront load. Alvarez documented the same rationale. Neither advisor asked the Donovans about investments held at other firms. After both investments were made, the Donovans had $270,000 (15% of combined assets) in illiquid non-traded REITs. Each individual account had 15% in non-traded REITs. In early 2024, both REITs suspended distributions due to declining commercial real estate valuations, and the Donovans, needing liquidity for an unexpected medical expense, could not access $270,000 of their savings.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: For Firm A (RIA - Karen Webb): Investment Advisers Act of 1940 fiduciary duty, as interpreted in SEC Release No. IA-5248 (Commission Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers, June 2019); duty of care requires reasonable inquiry into client's full financial situation including household investments. For Firm B (Broker-Dealer - Tom Alvarez): Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation requiring reasonable diligence, care, and skill, including understanding the retail customer's investment profile; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) to the extent it remains applicable alongside Reg BI; FINRA Regulatory Notice 15-02 (providing guidance on non-traded REIT concentration limits and due diligence requirements). Additionally, many state securities regulators impose specific concentration limits (often 10% of net worth) for non-traded REITs under state suitability standards adopted pursuant to NASAA guidelines.
src_correct_answer: Both advisors likely violated their respective obligations, though the analysis differs by advisor type and the violations are more nuanced than they appear. For Karen Webb at Firm A (the RIA): As an investment adviser, Webb owes a fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The fiduciary duty includes a duty of care requiring her to provide advice in the client's best interest based on a reasonable understanding of the client's full financial picture. The failure to inquire about Patricia's spouse's investments at other firms, particularly when she knew Patricia was married with shared financial goals and a joint retirement timeline, represents a failure in the duty of care. A 15% allocation to a single illiquid non-traded REIT with a 12% upfront load is aggressive for someone 7 years from retirement, and the failure to understand the household's total illiquid exposure amplifies this concern. For Tom Alvarez at Firm B (the broker-dealer): The transaction occurred in September 2022, well after Regulation Best Interest's June 30, 2020 compliance date. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), Alvarez must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making the recommendation. This includes understanding the customer's investment profile. While Reg BI does not explicitly require inquiry into a spouse's holdings at other firms in all cases, the Care Obligation requires understanding the customer's 'other investments' and 'financial situation.' For a married client with shared retirement goals, failing to ask about household investments is a deficiency. Additionally, both advisors should be scrutinized under their firms' own concentration policies. Many firms cap non-traded REIT exposure at 10% of net worth (excluding home equity). At the individual account level, each was at 15%, which may exceed firm concentration limits. The 11-12% upfront loads also demand heightened scrutiny — the Donovans paid approximately $31,000 in upfront costs on these investments. However, standing alone, each advisor's recommendation of 15% in a non-traded REIT for a client with a 7-year horizon, moderate risk tolerance, and $900,000 in assets is at the outer edge but potentially defensible if that were the client's only illiquid investment. The violation crystallizes from the failure of both advisors to conduct adequate inquiry into the household's complete financial picture, which would have revealed the concentration risk.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial for multiple reasons. First, the multi-party structure means each advisor's recommendation appears independently reasonable — 15% in a non-traded REIT for a moderate-risk client with a 7-year horizon is within commonly cited concentration guidelines. A general LLM might evaluate each recommendation in isolation and find no violation. Second, the two advisors are at different types of firms (RIA vs. broker-dealer), triggering different legal standards (fiduciary duty vs. Reg BI), which many models conflate. Third, the question of whether an advisor must inquire about a spouse's investments at a different firm is genuinely debatable and requires nuanced understanding of the 'investment profile' and 'financial situation' components of both the fiduciary standard and Reg BI. Fourth, the 12% and 11% upfront loads on non-traded REITs are high but were typical industry practice for these products, creating ambiguity about whether the cost alone is a violation.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely either (a) find no violation because each advisor's individual recommendation of 15% allocation appears within reasonable bounds for the client's profile and time horizon, missing the household concentration issue and the failure to inquire about outside holdings; or (b) find a violation but apply the wrong standard uniformly to both advisors (e.g., applying Reg BI to the RIA or applying fiduciary duty to the broker-dealer), and focus primarily on the upfront load rather than the more subtle inquiry failure.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Ellison, age 58, retired schoolteacher with a $420,000 IRA and $95,000 in a taxable brokerage account, had been a client of broker David Chen at Ridgeline Securities since 2014. Her account documents from 2014 listed her investment objective as 'income with moderate growth,' risk tolerance as 'moderate,' annual income of $52,000 (then still working), liquid net worth of $500,000, and investment experience as 'limited — mutual funds and CDs only.' In March 2019, Margaret attended a free dinner seminar hosted by David where he discussed using covered call strategies to generate income in retirement. She expressed interest. David updated her account profile in April 2019 to reflect 'options experience: 1 year (educational),' changed her investment objective to 'income and speculation,' and obtained her signature on options agreement paperwork approving her for Level 2 options trading (covered calls and cash-secured puts). Between May 2019 and January 2020, David executed 34 covered call transactions on blue-chip stocks in her IRA, generating approximately $18,400 in premium income. The trades were all covered calls on diversified large-cap positions she already held. Starting in February 2020, as markets became volatile, David began writing cash-secured puts on individual tech stocks in her taxable account — 12 transactions total through June 2020. Three of these puts were assigned, requiring Margaret to purchase $67,000 worth of volatile tech stocks at above-market prices, resulting in unrealized losses of $23,000. Margaret's brokerage account paperwork was updated again in June 2020 during the firm's annual review, but this time a new comprehensive account form was used by Ridgeline Securities that included a 'customer investment profile' section with more granular risk questions. Margaret filled out the new form indicating risk tolerance as 'conservative,' time horizon as '5-10 years,' and stating her primary goal was 'preservation of retirement savings.' David continued writing cash-secured puts in her taxable account through September 2020, adding 6 more transactions. The firm had adopted new transaction-level review procedures effective June 1, 2020, replacing its prior account-level review approach for recommendations.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) for transactions before June 30, 2020; SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation, for transactions on or after June 30, 2020; FINRA Rule 2360 (Options) regarding ongoing appropriateness of options trading; FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)
src_correct_answer: Yes, there are violations, but the analysis differs by time period due to the regulatory transition. For transactions before June 30, 2020, FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) applies. The covered call transactions in the IRA (May 2019–January 2020) are likely suitable — covered calls on existing diversified blue-chip holdings for income generation are generally consistent with a moderate-risk, income-oriented profile, and Level 2 options approval was obtained. However, the cash-secured puts on volatile individual tech stocks in the taxable account (February–June 2020) raise serious suitability concerns even under Rule 2111, because Margaret's original profile indicated limited experience and moderate risk tolerance, and writing puts on volatile tech stocks obligated her to purchase securities inconsistent with her profile. The profile update in April 2019 adding 'speculation' as an objective appears to have been engineered to justify the options strategy rather than reflecting a genuine change in customer circumstances, which implicates FINRA Rule 2111's customer-specific suitability obligation and potentially FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor). For transactions on or after June 30, 2020, Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) under the Securities Exchange Act Rule 15l-1 applies. The June 2020 updated profile explicitly showed Margaret as conservative with a preservation goal. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)), David was required to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the risks, rewards, and costs of each recommended transaction and have a reasonable basis to believe each recommendation was in Margaret's best interest at the time, considering her updated investment profile. Continuing to write cash-secured puts after June 2020 on her newly documented conservative profile is a clear violation of Reg BI's Care Obligation. Additionally, under FINRA Rule 2360 (Options), the firm has a continuing obligation to ensure options trading remains appropriate given updated customer information. The firm's failure to restrict options activity after the June 2020 profile update showing conservative risk tolerance also implicates supervisory obligations under FINRA Rules 3110 and 2360(b)(16). The key temporal trap is that the standard of care shifted mid-conduct from suitability to best interest, and the June 2020 profile update created an unambiguous factual record making the continued put-writing indefensible under either standard.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because it spans the June 30, 2020 Reg BI implementation date, requiring the model to apply different standards to different transactions by the same advisor in the same account. A general LLM might either apply only the old suitability standard to all transactions, or only Reg BI, rather than bifurcating the analysis. Additionally, the covered calls in the IRA are likely compliant (trapping models that say everything was a violation), while the cash-secured puts are problematic under both regimes but for slightly different analytical reasons. The profile update in June 2020 creates a factual pivot point that changes the analysis for post-June transactions — models may miss that the updated profile makes previously arguable trades clearly impermissible. The manufactured profile change in April 2019 is a subtle but important violation that models may overlook because the advisor technically did 'update the profile.'
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely either (1) find all options transactions violated suitability because Margaret was a retired schoolteacher with limited experience, ignoring that covered calls on existing blue-chip holdings can be appropriate for income-oriented moderate-risk investors, or (2) apply a single uniform standard across the entire time period without recognizing the Reg BI transition date, or (3) find no violation because the advisor obtained options approval paperwork and updated the customer profile, treating the formal documentation as dispositive.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Chen, age 72, retired schoolteacher with a $340,000 IRA account, walked into a branch office of Apex Wealth Partners on May 15, 2020. Her account profile listed her as conservative risk tolerance, income-oriented objective, 10-year time horizon, and liquid net worth of $80,000 outside the IRA. Her advisor, Brian Kowalski, had been her broker since 2015. On June 1, 2020, Brian recommended she invest $68,000 (20% of her IRA) into a non-traded REIT called Heartland Senior Living REIT, which had a 7-year lockup period with no early redemption program. The REIT offered a 6.5% stated distribution rate and invested in senior living facilities. Brian documented in his notes that he believed the aging demographics of the U.S. made senior housing a strong sector, that the 6.5% yield was attractive compared to the 0.5% she was earning on CDs, and that the 20% allocation left 80% of her portfolio in liquid assets. He ran a suitability review using the firm's checklist, which had not been updated since January 2019. The firm had sent an internal memo on March 1, 2020, reminding advisors that their obligations to retail customers had changed effective June 30, 2020, and that advisors should begin transitioning their practices accordingly. Brian made the recommendation on June 1, 2020, and the trade settled on June 5, 2020. Margaret received the prospectus and signed all required documents. By December 2021, the REIT suspended distributions and Margaret could not access her $68,000. She filed a complaint in February 2022.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — specifically FINRA Rule 2111(a) requiring that a recommended transaction be suitable based on the customer's investment profile including age, financial situation, needs, tax status, investment objectives, investment experience, investment time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance; FINRA Rule 2111.03 (recommended strategies); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 (suitability of complex products for senior investors); FINRA Regulatory Notice 15-02 (non-traded REITs). Note: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) compliance date was June 30, 2020 and does NOT apply to this June 1, 2020 recommendation.
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation, but the analysis depends critically on timing. The trade was recommended and executed on June 1-5, 2020, which is BEFORE the June 30, 2020 compliance date for Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1). Therefore, the applicable standard at the time of the recommendation was FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), not Reg BI. Under FINRA Rule 2111, Brian needed reasonable-basis suitability (understanding the product), customer-specific suitability (matching to Margaret's profile), and quantitative suitability. The recommendation fails customer-specific suitability under Rule 2111. Margaret is 72 years old, conservative, income-oriented, with only $80,000 in liquid assets outside the IRA. A 7-year lockup non-traded REIT consuming 20% of her retirement account is problematic for several reasons: (1) At age 72, a 7-year lockup means she would be 79 before accessing these funds, which is unreasonable for a retiree who may need funds for healthcare; (2) Her liquid net worth outside the IRA is only $80,000, meaning an unexpected expense could create financial hardship; (3) Non-traded REITs carry significant risks including illiquidity, lack of transparency, and distribution sustainability risk that are inconsistent with a conservative profile. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 specifically warned about concentration in illiquid products for elderly investors. FINRA Notice 15-02 further addressed concerns about non-traded REITs including that stated distribution rates can be misleading. Even under the pre-Reg BI suitability standard, this recommendation was unsuitable. The firm's failure to update its suitability checklist since January 2019, while not directly Brian's fault, contributed to the inadequate review process. However, a broker cannot hide behind a deficient firm checklist — the individual obligation under Rule 2111 is independent.
src_why_adversarial: This is a temporal trap because a general LLM will likely analyze the case under Reg BI (which became effective June 30, 2020) rather than FINRA Rule 2111, which was the applicable standard when the trade occurred on June 1, 2020. The firm's internal memo about transitioning to the new standard by June 30 creates a red herring — advisory firms were told to prepare, but the legal obligation had not yet taken effect. Many LLMs will apply the Reg BI Care Obligation and Component Obligations rather than the three-pronged FINRA suitability framework. Critically, the outcome is the same (violation), but the legal reasoning, applicable standard, and specific rule citations are entirely different. An LLM that gets the standard wrong would produce an analysis that is substantively incorrect even if the conclusion happens to be right. Some sophisticated LLMs might even incorrectly argue no violation occurred because the firm was 'in transition' to the new standard.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely analyze this under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) and its Care Obligation, citing the requirement to consider reasonably available alternatives, costs, and risks. It would reference the SEC's adopting release for Reg BI and potentially discuss the conflict of interest obligations. While the conclusion of 'violation' might be the same, the entire legal framework would be wrong — this trade predates Reg BI's compliance date and must be analyzed solely under FINRA Rule 2111 suitability requirements.

src_fact_pattern: Margaret Holloway, age 72, retired schoolteacher, had a $450,000 brokerage account with Lakeshore Securities since 2011. Her account documents consistently listed her risk tolerance as 'conservative,' her investment objective as 'income with preservation of capital,' her annual income as $38,000 from pension and Social Security, her liquid net worth as $510,000, and her investment experience as 'limited — primarily CDs and government bonds.' In April 2019, her longtime broker, Daniel Oates, recommended she invest $67,500 (15% of her portfolio) into the GulfStream Energy Corp 8.75% Senior Unsecured Notes due 2026, rated BB- by one major rating agency and B+ by another. Daniel prepared a detailed internal memorandum analyzing the bond, noting the company's improving cash flows, favorable oil price environment, the bond's relatively short duration, and the attractive yield spread over Treasuries. He documented that Mrs. Holloway needed additional income to cover rising medical expenses and that the bond's 8.75% coupon would generate approximately $5,906 annually. He also documented that the position represented only 15% of her portfolio, with the remainder in investment-grade municipal bonds and Treasury securities. Mrs. Holloway signed a general acknowledgment form stating she understood the recommendation. Daniel did not specifically explain the credit risk associated with below-investment-grade debt, the potential for significant principal loss, or the limited liquidity of high-yield bonds in distressed markets. By March 2020, GulfStream Energy's bonds had fallen to 41 cents on the dollar amid the oil price crash, and Mrs. Holloway's position lost approximately $39,800 in market value. She filed a complaint in June 2020 alleging the recommendation was inappropriate for her profile.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — specifically the customer-specific suitability obligation under Rule 2111(a) and supplementary material at Rule 2111.05(a); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Know Your Customer and Suitability); FINRA Notice to Members 04-89 (Non-Investment Grade Debt Securities); NASD Rule 2310 (predecessor suitability rule, for historical context). Note: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1) was not yet effective for this April 2019 transaction (compliance date June 30, 2020).
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation, and the analysis turns critically on which standard applies based on timing. The recommendation was made in April 2019, which is before the June 30, 2020 compliance date for Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) under the Exchange Act Rule 15l-1. Therefore, the applicable standard is the FINRA suitability framework under FINRA Rule 2111. Under Rule 2111, there are three component obligations: reasonable-basis suitability, customer-specific suitability, and quantitative suitability. While Daniel Oates appears to have performed reasonable-basis analysis (the internal memo analyzing GulfStream's fundamentals), the customer-specific suitability obligation was violated. FINRA Rule 2111.05(a) and related guidance make clear that a recommendation must be consistent with the customer's stated investment profile, including risk tolerance, investment objectives, and financial situation. A 72-year-old retired investor with conservative risk tolerance, an income-with-preservation objective, limited investment experience confined to CDs and government bonds, and modest income is not a suitable candidate for below-investment-grade high-yield corporate debt, which carries material credit risk, price volatility, and liquidity risk. Additionally, FINRA has specifically addressed high-yield bonds in Regulatory Notice 12-03, emphasizing heightened suitability obligations for complex or risky products, and in Notice to Members 04-89 regarding non-investment-grade debt securities, which requires that brokers make affirmative efforts to ensure conservative investors understand the risks. The fact that Daniel did not specifically explain credit risk, principal loss potential, or liquidity limitations further compounds the violation. Even under the pre-Reg BI suitability standard, the mere existence of a signed general acknowledgment form does not cure a fundamentally unsuitable recommendation. The 15% concentration, while not extreme in isolation, is significant for a conservative retiree whose entire investment experience is limited to the safest fixed-income instruments. Had this recommendation been made after June 30, 2020, Reg BI's Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) and Disclosure Obligation would have imposed even stricter requirements, including consideration of reasonably available alternatives and full disclosure of material risks.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial for multiple reasons. First, the temporal element is critical: a general LLM may incorrectly apply Reg BI to an April 2019 recommendation, when in fact the FINRA Rule 2111 suitability standard governed. Second, the advisor's detailed internal memorandum and the 15% allocation create a strong surface appearance of compliance — the advisor 'did his homework' and kept the position relatively modest. Third, many LLMs may focus on the reasonable-basis analysis and conclude the recommendation was suitable because the advisor documented his rationale. The trap is that customer-specific suitability is a separate, independent obligation that was clearly violated regardless of how thorough the product-level research was. Fourth, the signed acknowledgment form may mislead an LLM into thinking the customer consented to the risk, but a general acknowledgment does not satisfy the broker's independent suitability obligation under FINRA rules.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely say this is technically compliant or a borderline case, reasoning that the advisor conducted thorough research (documented memo), kept the allocation to only 15% of the portfolio, the bond had a relatively short maturity, the client had a legitimate need for income to cover medical expenses, and the client signed an acknowledgment. Some LLMs might also incorrectly apply Reg BI's disclosure framework and conclude the acknowledgment satisfied the standard.

src_fact_pattern: Robert Stein, age 47, is a practicing orthopedic surgeon in Charlotte, North Carolina, earning approximately $620,000 per year. He has a net worth of $4.8 million, including $1.9 million in retirement accounts, a $1.2 million home (with $400,000 remaining on the mortgage), $950,000 in taxable brokerage accounts diversified across equities and bonds, and $310,000 in cash and money market funds. Robert has been investing for over 20 years and holds a moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance. His investment objectives are long-term growth and income diversification. He told his advisor, Linda Chao, that he was interested in adding real estate exposure to his portfolio and was comfortable with a 7-10 year time horizon for a portion of his investments. After a detailed discussion and review of Robert's complete financial picture, Linda recommended that he invest $100,000 — approximately 2.1% of his net worth — into a non-traded REIT focused on institutional-quality commercial properties. The REIT carried a front-end load of 5.75%, a minimum holding period of five years, and limited quarterly redemption opportunities thereafter. Linda provided Robert with the prospectus, a detailed summary of risks including illiquidity, and a comparison with publicly traded REIT alternatives. She documented in her notes that Robert understood the illiquidity, the fee structure, and the long holding period, and that he preferred the non-traded REIT's lower volatility profile compared to publicly traded REITs. Robert signed an acknowledgment confirming his understanding of the product's features and risks. The investment represented a small allocation within a well-diversified portfolio, and Robert maintained ample liquidity in his other accounts to meet any foreseeable financial needs.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer:
No, Linda Chao appears to have acted in compliance with applicable standards.

**Reg BI — Care Obligation:**
Under Regulation Best Interest, the Care Obligation requires that the advisor exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill, and have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest. Here, Linda conducted a thorough review of Robert's financial situation, including his income, net worth, liquidity, time horizon, risk tolerance, and investment objectives. Robert is a high-income, high-net-worth investor with a long time horizon (7-10 years), moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, and an expressed interest in real estate diversification. The $100,000 investment represents only 2.1% of his net worth and does not create dangerous concentration or threaten his liquidity.

**Cost Consideration:**
While the 5.75% front-end load is significant, Linda addressed this by presenting alternatives (publicly traded REIT ETFs) and documenting that Robert understood the cost structure and made an informed choice based on his preference for the non-traded REIT's lower day-to-day price volatility. Under Reg BI, the advisor must consider cost but is not required to recommend the lowest-cost option if there is a reasonable basis for the recommendation.

**FINRA Rule 2111 — All Three Suitability Obligations:**
Reasonable-basis suitability is satisfied because non-traded REITs are legitimate investment products suitable for certain investors; Linda understood the product's characteristics. Customer-specific suitability is met because Robert's profile — high income, substantial net worth, long time horizon, moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, interest in real estate, and ample remaining liquidity — is consistent with a small allocation to an illiquid real estate product. Quantitative suitability is not at issue since this is a single, modest allocation.

**Documentation:**
Linda's thorough documentation — including notes of the discussion, risk disclosures, product comparisons, and Robert's signed acknowledgment — demonstrates the care and diligence expected under both Reg BI and FINRA suitability standards.

**Likely Regulatory Outcome:**
No violation would be found. This represents a well-considered, well-documented recommendation of an illiquid product to a sophisticated, high-net-worth investor for whom it constitutes a small, diversifying allocation within an otherwise liquid and well-diversified portfolio.

src_fact_pattern: Robert Galloway, age 58, is a mid-level corporate manager earning $135,000 annually. In January 2024, he met with his financial advisor, Karen Whitfield, at a broker-dealer. Robert had $410,000 in a traditional IRA rollover from a previous employer's 401(k), invested in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index mutual funds with a blended expense ratio of 0.12%. Robert told Karen he was concerned about market volatility as he approached retirement in 7 years and wanted more predictable income. He was not particularly tax-savvy and did not raise any questions about tax treatment. Karen recommended that Robert move $300,000 of his IRA into a variable annuity with a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit (GLWB) rider. The annuity had the following features: annual mortality and expense charge of 1.15%, administrative fee of 0.10%, underlying sub-account expenses averaging 0.75%, and the GLWB rider cost of 1.05% annually — for a total all-in annual cost of approximately 3.05%. The GLWB guaranteed a 5% withdrawal rate for life beginning at age 65, regardless of market performance. The annuity had a 7-year declining surrender charge schedule starting at 7% in year one. Karen's firm received a 5.5% upfront commission on the annuity sale. Karen documented the following rationale: Robert expressed concern about market volatility; the GLWB addresses his desire for predictable retirement income; the 7-year surrender schedule aligns with his 7-year time horizon to retirement; Robert's overall portfolio still has $110,000 in low-cost index funds for liquidity; and the guaranteed income feature provides value that justifies the higher costs. Karen did not document any analysis comparing the annuity's tax-deferral benefit to Robert's existing IRA tax-deferral, nor did she document consideration of lower-cost alternatives that could provide similar downside protection, such as a balanced fund with a bond allocation shift or a fixed indexed annuity with lower fees. Robert's IRA already provided full tax deferral on all gains.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), Care Obligation and Conflict of Interest Obligation; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55; NASD Notice to Members 99-35 (sales of variable annuities); FINRA Rule 2330 (Members' Responsibilities Regarding Deferred Variable Annuities), particularly Rule 2330(b) requiring reasonable basis to believe the customer would benefit from certain features of deferred variable annuities; SEC Regulation Best Interest Adopting Release (June 2019) discussion of cost as a relevant factor in the Care Obligation
src_correct_answer: Yes, Karen Whitfield violated applicable standards, though the analysis is more nuanced than the typical 'annuity in an IRA' scenario. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), the Care Obligation requires that the advisor evaluate reasonably available alternatives and that the recommendation reflect the retail customer's best interest without placing the advisor's financial interest ahead of the customer's. Under the specific Reg BI guidance regarding annuities in tax-advantaged accounts, placing a variable annuity inside a traditional IRA is not per se prohibited. The SEC and FINRA have long acknowledged (FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55; NASD Notice to Members 99-35) that tax deferral is only one feature of an annuity — other features like guaranteed income riders may independently justify the purchase even within a tax-deferred account. This is the knowledge trap: the violation is NOT simply because she placed an annuity inside an IRA. The violation exists because (1) Karen failed to conduct a reasonable comparative analysis of lower-cost alternatives that could address Robert's volatility concern — such as reallocating the existing low-cost portfolio toward a more conservative asset allocation, purchasing a fixed indexed annuity with substantially lower fees, or considering a single premium immediate annuity at retirement — and (2) the total cost differential is enormous: 3.05% annually versus 0.12%, meaning approximately $8,790 per year in additional costs on $300,000, which over 7 years (even before compounding) represents roughly $61,530 in additional costs that directly reduces Robert's retirement assets. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation, the advisor must consider costs as a factor and cannot recommend a higher-cost product without a reasonable basis for concluding the additional features justify the cost. The GLWB's 5% guaranteed withdrawal at age 65 on a $300,000 base provides $15,000 annually — but after 7 years of 3.05% in fees, the account value could be substantially diminished. Karen's documentation, while addressing some factors, critically omits any cost-benefit comparison or analysis of alternatives, which is required under the Reg BI Care and Disclosure Obligations. The 5.5% upfront commission also creates a conflict that must be addressed under the Conflict of Interest Obligation.
src_why_adversarial: This is a knowledge trap because the obvious answer — 'annuity inside an IRA is always a violation because tax deferral is redundant' — is actually wrong as a categorical rule. Many LLMs have learned this oversimplified heuristic. FINRA and the SEC have explicitly acknowledged that annuity features beyond tax deferral (like GLWBs) can justify placement in an IRA. A sophisticated LLM might therefore overcorrect and say 'no violation because the GLWB provides independent value beyond tax deferral.' The actual violation is more subtle: it's the failure to conduct and document a cost-benefit analysis against reasonably available lower-cost alternatives, and the failure to establish that the specific GLWB benefit justifies a ~2.93% annual cost increase. The trap catches both unsophisticated models (wrong reason for violation) and sophisticated models (overcorrecting to no violation).
src_common_wrong_answer: Either (1) 'Clear violation because placing a tax-deferred annuity inside an already tax-deferred IRA provides no additional tax benefit and is inherently unsuitable' — which is an oversimplification and wrong legal standard, or (2) 'No violation because the GLWB rider provides guaranteed income independent of tax deferral, the surrender schedule matches the time horizon, and Karen documented a reasonable rationale' — which ignores the cost-comparison and alternatives analysis requirements.

src_fact_pattern: David and Sharon Kowalski, both age 58 and working as a postal carrier and dental hygienist respectively, had a combined household income of approximately $112,000. In January 2021, they consolidated $410,000 from several old 401(k) accounts into a single advisory account at Pinnacle Wealth Partners, managed by advisor Rachel Fontaine. Fontaine placed the couple into a wrap-fee advisory program charging 1.35% annually on assets under management, which amounted to approximately $5,535 per year in fees. Fontaine constructed an initial portfolio of 60% broad-market equity index ETFs, 30% investment-grade bond ETFs, and 10% in a money market fund. After the initial allocation was completed in February 2021, Fontaine made no changes to the portfolio for the next 32 months — through March 2024. During that entire period, there were zero rebalancing trades, zero tactical adjustments, and zero changes despite significant interest rate increases in 2022 and 2023, a bear market in equities in 2022, and the couple reaching age 60 and approaching their stated retirement target of age 62. The only account activity consisted of automatic dividend reinvestments. Over the 32-month period, the Kowalskis paid approximately $15,200 in cumulative advisory fees. Had the same portfolio been held in a commission-based brokerage account, the initial trades would have generated approximately $320 in commissions, and with no subsequent activity, no further commissions would have been charged — resulting in total costs of $320 versus $15,200. Fontaine's book of business contained 187 advisory accounts. An internal audit sampling revealed that 74 of those accounts — roughly 40% — had fewer than two discretionary trades in any rolling 12-month period. Fontaine's annual advisory fee revenue was approximately $620,000, while her estimated commission equivalent revenue from the same activity level would have been under $28,000. The Kowalskis received two brief annual review emails from Fontaine during the period, each consisting of a one-paragraph summary stating 'your portfolio remains on track' with no substantive analysis, no updated risk assessment, and no discussion of their approaching retirement date.
src_red_flag: Clients paying ongoing asset-based advisory fees for a dormant, unmanaged portfolio where the fee-based structure costs dramatically more than a commission alternative with no commensurate advisory services being provided
src_red_flag_indicators: ["Zero discretionary trades or rebalancing over a 32-month period despite significant market events including a bear market and major interest rate shifts", "Cumulative advisory fees of $15,200 compared to an estimated $320 in equivalent commission-based costs — a 47-to-1 cost disparity", "No updated risk assessment or retirement planning discussion as clients aged from 58 to 60 and approached their stated retirement target of age 62", "Annual review communications were perfunctory one-paragraph emails with no substantive analysis or portfolio recommendations", "Internal audit revealed 40% of the advisor's 187 accounts showed minimal trading activity (fewer than two trades per year), suggesting a systemic pattern", "Advisor's annual fee revenue of $620,000 was approximately 22 times what equivalent commission-based compensation would have been, indicating the fee-based model is not aligned with service delivery", "The portfolio's static 60/30/10 allocation was never adjusted as the clients' time horizon shortened and market conditions changed materially", "Accounts were originally consolidated from 401(k) plans through an IRA rollover, raising questions about whether the rollover recommendation itself was in the clients' interest given the fee structure"]
src_regulatory_concern: Reverse churning implicates Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), 17 CFR § 240.15l-1, specifically the Care Obligation, which requires broker-dealers to evaluate reasonably available alternatives including account type and whether a commission-based account would be more cost-effective given the anticipated level of trading activity. For investment advisers, the fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1) and 206(2), requires advisers to act in clients' best interests and not place their own financial interests ahead of clients', including the obligation to recommend the most appropriate account type. FINRA Regulatory Notice 13-23 addresses reverse churning concerns in fee-based accounts. The lack of ongoing portfolio management despite collecting advisory fees may also constitute a breach of the duty to provide continuous and regular supervisory or management services as represented in Form ADV disclosures, potentially violating the antifraud provisions. Additionally, the IRA rollover from 401(k) plans triggers analysis under the Department of Labor's prohibited transaction exemptions (PTE 2020-02), which requires documentation that the rollover recommendation is in the retirement investor's best interest, including a comparison of fees.
src_recommended_action: Pinnacle Wealth Partners' compliance department should conduct an immediate firm-wide review of all advisory accounts to identify those with minimal trading activity relative to fees charged, using a quantitative screen for accounts with fewer than a defined threshold of discretionary trades per year. For the Kowalski account and the 74 flagged accounts, the firm should perform a cost-benefit analysis comparing advisory fees paid against what commission-based costs would have been, and assess whether the level of advisory services delivered (financial planning, rebalancing, tax management, retirement analysis) justified the fee-based structure. Clients who were materially disadvantaged should receive restitution of excess fees — for the Kowalskis, approximately $14,880 representing the difference between fees paid and commission equivalents. Fontaine should be placed on heightened supervision with mandatory quarterly documentation of advisory services delivered to each client. The firm should implement automated surveillance to flag advisory accounts with dormant activity for quarterly compliance review. The firm should also consider whether Fontaine's Form ADV brochure accurately describes the services provided and amend disclosures if necessary. If the pattern reflects willful neglect of fiduciary duties, referral to state securities regulators and SEC examination staff is warranted.

src_fact_pattern: Carlos and Elena Gutierrez, both age 58, are dual-income professionals earning a combined $285,000 annually. They have a joint brokerage account at Pacifica Wealth Partners with a total value of $1.8 million. Their stated investment objectives are 'growth and income,' their risk tolerance is 'moderate to high,' and their time horizon is '10+ years.' They have an additional $600,000 in employer retirement plans, own their home free of mortgage ($550,000 value), and maintain a $95,000 emergency fund in a bank savings account. Their total net worth, excluding primary residence, is approximately $2.5 million. Their financial advisor, Rachel Yamamoto (Series 7, Series 66), recommended a $360,000 investment (20% of their brokerage account) in a non-traded real estate investment trust (REIT) focused on commercial office properties. The REIT had a 7-year expected hold period, paid a 5.8% annual distribution, carried a front-end load of 8.5%, and had no secondary market for shares — redemption was limited to a quarterly share repurchase program capped at 2.5% of outstanding shares per quarter, at the board's discretion. Rachel thoroughly explained the illiquidity, the fee structure, the fact that distributions might include return of capital, the concentration in commercial office space, and the risks of the sector including remote work trends. She documented all disclosures in a signed acknowledgment form. She also verified that the Gutierrezes met the accredited investor net worth and income thresholds. The couple confirmed they understood all risks and signed all documents. Rachel checked the REIT sponsor's track record — three prior programs with average annualized returns of 6.2% to investors. Pacifica Wealth Partners' internal policy, documented in its written supervisory procedures manual updated six months prior, states that 'non-traded REITs and other illiquid alternative investments shall not exceed 10% of a client's liquid net worth, defined as total net worth excluding primary residence.' No exception process is documented. The branch manager, Tom Fielding, reviewed and approved the transaction, noting the clients' high income, strong net worth, and moderate-to-high risk tolerance.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1, specifically the Care Obligation (§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) and the Compliance Obligation (§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iv)); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) and FINRA Rule 3120 (Supervisory Control System); FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 (Obligation of Broker-Dealers to Conduct Reasonable Investigations in Regulation D Offerings); NASAA Omnibus Guidelines — Statement of Policy Regarding Real Estate Investment Trusts (non-traded REIT concentration limits, commonly 10% of liquid net worth); applicable state securities regulations on alternative investment concentration limits.
src_correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation, but the violation is subtle and primarily procedural/supervisory rather than rooted in the product's unsuitability for the clients' general profile. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and/or Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) depending on timing, the recommendation must be suitable/in the client's best interest. On its face, the recommendation appears reasonable: the Gutierrezes have high income, long time horizon, moderate-to-high risk tolerance, substantial liquid assets, and the non-traded REIT allocation is only 20% of their brokerage account. However, the critical violation arises from the firm's own internal concentration limit. Pacifica's written supervisory procedures cap illiquid alternative investments at 10% of liquid net worth (excluding primary residence). The Gutierrezes' liquid net worth is approximately $2.5 million ($1.8M brokerage + $600K retirement + $95K emergency savings, excluding $550K home). Ten percent of $2.5 million is $250,000. The $360,000 recommended investment exceeds this limit by $110,000 (44% over the cap). Under FINRA's supervisory framework (FINRA Rules 3110 and 3120), firms must establish, maintain, and enforce written supervisory procedures. When a firm establishes internal concentration limits as part of its supervisory system, those limits become enforceable standards. Exceeding them — even when the underlying recommendation might otherwise satisfy general suitability — constitutes a supervisory violation. Branch manager Tom Fielding's approval does not cure the deficiency because no documented exception process existed. Additionally, under Reg BI's Compliance Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iv)), broker-dealers must establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with the best interest standard. A firm that sets concentration limits but then approves transactions exceeding them without a formal exception process fails to enforce its own compliance framework. Furthermore, many states impose their own non-traded REIT concentration limits — commonly 10% of liquid net worth — through state securities regulations and the North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) guidelines for non-traded REITs. The advisor and branch manager may also have violated these state-level thresholds. The violation here is not that the product was categorically wrong for these clients, but that the firm's own guardrails were breached without proper process, which constitutes both a supervisory failure and a compliance obligation failure.
src_why_adversarial: This is extremely difficult because on every client-facing dimension, the recommendation looks solid: wealthy clients, high income, long time horizon, appropriate risk tolerance, thorough disclosure, documented acknowledgment, verified accredited investor status, and solid sponsor track record. A general LLM would almost certainly conclude 'no violation' because the product appears suitable for the clients' profile. The hidden deficiency is the firm's own internal concentration limit — a detail buried in the fact pattern that requires the model to (1) calculate liquid net worth correctly by excluding the primary residence, (2) apply the 10% cap, (3) recognize that the $360,000 investment exceeds the $250,000 limit, and (4) understand that violating a firm's own written supervisory procedures constitutes a regulatory violation even when the underlying recommendation is otherwise suitable. Most LLMs would not treat internal firm policies as creating enforceable regulatory obligations.
src_common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would almost certainly find no violation, reasoning that the clients are wealthy, sophisticated, have appropriate risk tolerance and time horizon, were fully informed of all risks, signed acknowledgment forms, meet accredited investor standards, and the 20% allocation to a single alternative investment is within commonly discussed diversification norms. The model would likely praise the thorough disclosure and documentation as evidence of compliance, completely missing the firm's internal concentration limit breach and the supervisory/compliance obligation implications.

src_fact_pattern: Mei-Ling Park, age 44, is a pediatric nurse earning $82,000 per year in Portland, Oregon. She is a single mother of two children, ages 10 and 14, and is saving for their college education as well as her own retirement. She has $145,000 in a 401(k) from a prior employer, $38,000 in a savings account, and $22,000 in a 529 education plan. When Mei-Ling opened a brokerage account with advisor Craig Hollowell in January 2023, she filled out a risk tolerance questionnaire during an in-person meeting. She selected 'moderate' risk tolerance, indicated her investment timeline was 10–15 years, and wrote in the objectives section: 'growth for retirement and college savings, but I can't afford big losses because this is all I have.' During the meeting, Hollowell suggested that her answers were 'too conservative for someone her age' and encouraged her to change her risk profile to 'aggressive growth.' He told her, 'You have plenty of time to recover from any downturns — you should be more aggressive.' Mei-Ling hesitated but ultimately agreed to change the form after Hollowell's repeated urging. With the aggressive profile now on file, Hollowell placed her $145,000 rollover IRA into a concentrated portfolio: $55,000 in small-cap growth stocks, $40,000 in sector-specific technology ETFs, $30,000 in options-based income strategies involving covered calls and cash-secured puts, and $20,000 in a single-stock position in a pre-revenue biotech company that Hollowell described as 'a sure winner.' Hollowell earned approximately $4,200 in commissions on the initial trades. By December 2023, the biotech stock had fallen 80% after a failed clinical trial, the options strategies produced losses of $11,000, and the overall portfolio was down approximately $48,000, or 33%.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_answer: Craig Hollowell committed several serious violations. First and most critically, he improperly manipulated the customer's risk profile. Under FINRA Rule 2111 and its supplementary materials, a broker cannot substitute his own judgment for the customer's actual risk tolerance. When Mei-Ling initially indicated a moderate risk tolerance and specifically stated she could not afford big losses, that was her genuine investment profile. Hollowell pressured her to change the form to 'aggressive growth,' which constituted a manipulation of the customer's documented risk profile to justify pre-determined, unsuitable recommendations. FINRA has been clear in enforcement actions and guidance that a broker cannot override or pressure a client to change their stated risk tolerance to facilitate aggressive recommendations. Even with the altered form, the customer-specific suitability obligation under FINRA Rule 2111 requires that the recommendation be suitable based on the customer's actual financial situation and needs — not a coerced risk profile. Mei-Ling is a single mother with moderate income, limited liquid assets, dual savings goals (college and retirement), and no prior experience with complex instruments. The concentration in small-cap growth, sector ETFs, options strategies, and a single pre-revenue biotech stock was inconsistent with her true moderate profile and her explicit statement about being unable to absorb large losses. Under Regulation Best Interest, the Care Obligation requires that the broker consider the customer's actual investment profile. The manipulation of the risk questionnaire does not insulate the broker — the substance of the customer's financial circumstances and stated concerns controls. Placing $20,000 (nearly 14% of the rollover) into a single pre-revenue biotech stock with binary clinical trial risk violated the reasonable-basis suitability obligation, as this is a speculative position unsuitable even for many aggressive investors at that concentration level. The options strategies introduced additional complexity that Mei-Ling, with no stated options experience, could not reasonably be expected to understand. Under Reg BI's Disclosure Obligation, Hollowell was required to provide full and fair disclosure of risks; describing the biotech stock as 'a sure winner' was materially misleading. The Conflict of Interest Obligation is also implicated given the $4,200 in commissions generated by the active trading strategy. Regulatory consequences would likely be severe: the manipulation of the risk profile is considered a particularly egregious violation. Likely outcomes include restitution, disgorgement of commissions, significant fines, and a lengthy suspension or bar. The firm's supervisory systems under FINRA Rule 3110 would also be examined for failing to identify the risk profile change and the resulting mismatch between the customer's actual circumstances and the trading activity.

src_fact_pattern: Carlos Medina, age 44, is a software engineer earning $195,000 per year with $1.2 million in investable assets across three accounts: a $500,000 brokerage account at Summit Securities, a $400,000 401(k) at his employer, and a $300,000 Roth IRA at another firm. Carlos is an active trader who executes approximately 200 trades per year in his Summit Securities brokerage account. He has 18 years of trading experience, subscribes to three financial research services, and previously held a Series 7 license when he worked briefly at a brokerage firm in 2006-2008 before transitioning to software engineering. In January 2023, Carlos sent a detailed email to his advisor at Summit Securities, Rachel Fong, requesting that she purchase $75,000 worth of the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3x Shares (SOXL) in his brokerage account. In the email, Carlos explained his thesis: he believed the semiconductor sector would see sustained upward momentum over the next 8-10 months due to AI demand and that the 3x leverage would amplify his returns. He explicitly stated he understood the daily reset mechanism and compounding decay but believed the strong directional trend would overcome any volatility drag. Rachel reviewed Carlos's account profile, noted his extensive trading history, high income, significant overall net worth, experience with options and leveraged products (he had previously traded 2x leveraged ETFs successfully), and his former licensure. She executed the trade. She did not, however, provide Carlos with the leveraged ETF's prospectus or the firm's standardized risk disclosure document specific to leveraged and inverse products, which Summit Securities' written supervisory procedures require to be delivered to all clients before the first leveraged ETF purchase in their account, regardless of client sophistication. Carlos had never previously purchased a leveraged ETF at Summit Securities specifically; his prior leveraged ETF trades were at another brokerage. Over the next seven months, SOXL increased approximately 68%, and Carlos sold the position in August 2023 for a profit of approximately $51,000. No complaint was filed.
src_question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
src_applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1 (Care Obligation and Compliance Obligation); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision, including requirement to enforce WSPs); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs); FINRA Regulatory Notice 22-08 (Complex Products and Options — Enhanced Sales Practice Obligations); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor)
src_correct_answer: Yes, Rachel Fong committed a violation, but it is a procedural/compliance violation rather than a substantive suitability violation. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), the Compliance Obligation requires broker-dealers to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI. Summit Securities' written supervisory procedures mandated delivery of the leveraged ETF prospectus and a firm-specific risk disclosure document prior to the first leveraged ETF purchase in the account. Rachel's failure to deliver these documents violates the firm's WSPs and, by extension, the Compliance Obligation component of Reg BI. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs) and FINRA Regulatory Notice 22-08 (Complex Products) emphasize that firms must have robust procedures for complex products including leveraged ETFs, and that these procedures must be followed regardless of client sophistication. The substantive suitability analysis under FINRA Rule 2111 (which remains applicable alongside Reg BI for product-specific suitability) and the Care Obligation of Reg BI would likely support the recommendation as substantively suitable given Carlos's profile: high income, substantial liquid net worth, extensive trading experience, former licensure, demonstrated knowledge of the product mechanics, and the position representing only about 6.25% of total investable assets. However, the procedural failure is independently actionable. The fact that the client was sophisticated, directed the trade himself, and ultimately profited does not cure the procedural deficiency. FINRA has consistently held that firms cannot waive compliance with their own written supervisory procedures based on client sophistication, and profitable outcomes do not retroactively validate procedural failures.
src_why_adversarial: This scenario is extremely tricky because it contains multiple elements that would lead a general LLM astray. First, the client is highly sophisticated, knowledgeable, directed the trade himself, and even articulated understanding of the daily reset mechanism — making it seem like no violation occurred. Second, the trade was profitable, which psychologically biases toward 'no violation.' Third, the position was reasonably sized relative to total assets. Fourth, the leveraged ETF holding period (7 months) is longer than typically recommended, but it worked out — creating a results-bias trap. The actual violation is buried in a single procedural detail: the firm's WSPs required pre-trade delivery of specific disclosure documents for the first leveraged ETF purchase in the account, and Rachel skipped this step. Most LLMs will focus entirely on the substantive suitability analysis (where no violation exists) and miss the procedural compliance failure, or will incorrectly conclude the holding period itself constitutes a violation even though the substantive recommendation was suitable.
src_common_wrong_answer: No violation. Carlos is a highly sophisticated investor with 18 years of experience, former industry licensure, and demonstrated understanding of leveraged ETF mechanics. He specifically directed the trade, the position represented a reasonable percentage of his portfolio, and the investment was profitable. The advisor appropriately evaluated the client's profile before executing the requested trade. A leveraged ETF recommendation to this particular client with this profile is substantively suitable.
